title: Generalized Antoine and Wagner Equations Consistent with the Predictions of the Peng-Robinson Equation of State Using Similarity Variables
abstract: Chemical engineers use the Antoine and Wagner vapor pressure equations because of their relative simplicity; however, their accuracy is limited to restricted temperature ranges and they require substance-specific constants. Generalized methods were developed to find Antoine and Wagner equation constants consistent with the Peng-Robinson (PR) equation of state. Two similarity variables were introduced to simplify calculations. Adjusted temperature, η, combined reduced temperature and acentric factor. Adjusted pressure, Ψ, combined reduced pressure and reduced temperature. A PR vapor pressure algorithm generated a data set of these similarity variables, and a nonlinear least squares method was used to find generalized Antoine constants. When all three generalized Antoine constants were independently fit, the results matched PR vapor pressure predictions within 0.05 percent for twelve subranges of adjusted temperatures from the critical point down to 0.23. Fitting only the C constant by least squares with the A and B constants calculated by exact fits of the adjusted pressure at the endpoints of each subrange, only five adjusted temperature subranges gave the desired accuracy from the critical point down to 0.23. For the Wagner equation, only three adjusted temperature subranges gave the desired accuracy from the critical point down to 0.23.

title: Uncertainty Analysis with Geothermal Techno-Economic Tool Geophires v2.0: Model Development, Validation and Case Studies
abstract: GEOPHIRES v2.0 is an open-source techno-economic simulator used for modeling geothermal reservoirs. One of the challenges in geothermal reservoir modeling is handling uncertain parameters that are difficult to measure or characterize. Over the course of this project, three modules have been developed for GEOPHIRES v2.0 to address uncertainty in geothermal parameters: multiparameter tornado diagram analysis, single parameter sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo analysis. These modules provide the user with tools to assess the impact of parameter uncertainty on the technical and economic performance of a geothermal system. High performance computing capabilities have also been implemented to effectively perform the large number of GEOPHIRES v2.0 simulations required for Monte Carlo analysis. A geothermal plant in Paris was used as a case study, first to validate the GEOPHIRES v2.0 tool by comparing the output with the results from the System Advisor Model (SAM) and actual plant performance, and secondly to test the three uncertainty analysis modules. The uncertainty analysis indicated that drilling costs and geothermal gradient have a major impact on overall plant levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) or heat (LCOH), while reservoir rock properties only have a minor impact.

title: Analysis of Model Application Using CFD in Transition Mixing
abstract: Mixing is a common practice used in a vast majority of industrial processing and manufacturing applications. Mixing is typically studied in either the laminar or turbulent flow regimes because the equations governing these regimes are well understood. Due to the complexity of transition mixing, minimal modeling is done in this regime. Certain industries naturally find themselves operating in and around the transition regime, but are unable to fully understand the process due to the inability of accurate modeling. The mixing of many personal care products fall into this category because they typically deal with complex non-Newtonian fluids. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is a tool that enables the modeling of various physical systems to analyze velocity profiles, streamlines, and numerous other fluid and flow parameters. Transient simulations of the mixing of Carbopol (a high molecular weight, crosslinked polyacrylic acid polymer) were run using CFD in order to compare the blend time results with real data. Analysis was done by looking at concentration profiles and volume fractions at various locations in the tank throughout the mixing process. The viscous models compared were the laminar and realizable k-epsilon. The mixture model was used to compare the two different phases identified by different dye color. The Carbopol viscosity was modeled using a non-Newtonian power law. The two different viscous models yield different blending results, neither of which match up with the real data, indicating a discrepancy between the models and mixing within the transition flow regime.

title: Nonlinear Dynamic System Identification of Monoclonal Antibody Production
abstract: The demand for monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) has increased due to their high affinity and specificity to thousands of biological targets. Immunotherapy using mAbs are widespread in the treatment of various diseases including cancer and autoimmune disorders. The entry of biosimilars (variations of previously approved mAbs with similar efficacy and safety to its predecessor) into the market creates a need for production process intensification, and computational models are valuable tools which can be used for optimizations purposes. In this work, we identify data driven models that simulate the system dynamics of mAb (IgG4 cB72.3) generation in GS-NS0 cells in a semi-batch operation. Hammerstein Wiener and Nonlinear AutoRegressive models with eXogeneous (NARX), a subclass of Recurrent Neural Networks, are fitted to simulated data and compared for performance. The trained data driven models demonstrate good accuracy and reduce computational cost in comparison to the rigorous dynamic model. This potentially makes the data-driven approach a versatile tool for computationally demanding optimization studies. Results favor the Hammerstein Wiener model for multiple simulation datasets, and the NARX model for a single simulation dataset. Further exploration is under progress to determine the best surrogate model, which can be used for process optimization. *The first and second authors contributed equally to this work.

title: Developing Matlab Code for Analysis of Heterogeneous Engineered Cardiac Tissue during Contraction
abstract: Title: Developing MATLAB Code for Analysis of Heterogeneous Engineered Cardiac Tissue during Contraction Primary Author (and presenter): Bush, Michaela, Z Additional Authors: Ellis, Morgan. Finklea, Ferdous. Lipke, Elizabeth Department: Department of Chemical Engineering College/School: Auburn University Description: Engineered cardiac tissue (ECT) is needed for treating various cardiovascular diseases, studying development and disease mechanisms, and for high-throughput drug screening, so we are producing ECT directly from human induced pluripotent stem cells. The ECT must have the appropriate phenotype, maturation, and functionality for downstream applications. One way we assess these properties of ECT is by analyzing the speed and duration of calcium propagation, necessary for cardiac function. Calcium propagation is measured using optical mapping; we record high-speed videos of ECT treated with a calcium-sensitive fluorescent dye that brightens in the presence of calcium, creating flashes that follow calcium propagation. The purpose of this project is to create a custom MATLAB ® program that can analyze these videos and extract the calcium transient duration (CTD), conduction velocity, and the heterogeneity index of the tissue. Due to the heterogeneous nature of 3D-ECT, not all pixels contain useable data. New features have been incorporated to remove unusable pixels based on their lower fluorescence or range. The program can filter data temporally to smooth the propagation waves and normalize it to remove variations in base fluorescence. Pixels that lack consistent propagation are then removed based on their dissimilarity to pixels with consistent propagation. From the remaining usable pixels, the number of calcium propagation events and the time these events occur is quantified and visualized using isochrone maps. The conduction velocity is calculated by choosing several pairs of points and calculating the time calcium travels between the points divided by the distance between the points. A new feature incorporating the MATLAB® gradient function allows direction of the velocity for groupings of pixels to be plotted to aid in visualization of the wave propagation and the optimal pairs that best represent the overall conduction velocity. A method of calculating the CTD, which measures the time between depolarization and repolarization, at any repolarization percentage was implemented using the luminosity at the peak and trough of each wave. The heterogeneity index measures the variance of the CTD which is relevant as cells in 3D-ECT are not distributed evenly. Using this data, we can determine the functionality of ECT and the quality of our current methods to create ECT.

title: Examining Potential Intermediates in the Electrochemical Synthesis of Ozone from Water
abstract: Ozone can be produced by electrochemical water oxidation, yet there are many questions about how to engineer its reaction mechanism that involves six electron transfer steps. Understanding this reaction can offer insight into properties of intermediates along the reaction pathway, which can influence the activation energies and rate determining step of this reaction. Once this information is known, it may be used to determine the properties of a catalyst, which can ultimately improve the rate and the energy cost for this reaction. To properly understand this reaction, it is imperative to have an accurate understanding of the energetics and thermodynamic properties (e.g. acidity constants and standard redox potentials) of hypothetical reaction intermediates along the reaction pathway. We have used Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) along with implicit and mixed solvation models to determine these acidity constants and reduction potentials for a collection of oxygen containing molecules. A mixed implicit/explicit solvation model and the accompanying thermodynamic cycle has also been found to reduce errors in calculations compared to the available experimental data. After benchmarking this approach with available experimental data, we predict thermodynamic properties for different solvated reaction intermediates and determine which are relevant for the electrochemical ozone production reaction.

title: A Comparison of Methods for Predicting the Melting Point of Perarylphosphonium and Perarylsulfonium Ionic Liquids Using Molecular Dynamics
abstract: Ionic liquids (ILs) are organic salts that have melting points below 100°C. Their unusual properties, such as non-flammability, negligible vapor pressure, and high tunability have made them of interest for industrial applications such as heat storage, fuel cells, and batteries. In most applications melting point is desired so that the IL remains pumpable at moderate temperature. Oftentimes the IL structure can be modified, which affects the melting point, however knowing what modifications must be made to lower the melting point remains a challenge. Molecular dynamics (MD) is a method to simulate the physical interactions and movements among a molecule and its atoms. Several different methods exist in MD to calculate the melting point of a compound; however, it is not entirely clear how well each of these methods perform for ionic liquids. Knowing which method performs the best would allow us to connect the changes in chemical structure of ILs with the melting point. In this work we compare the performance of three popular methods for computing the melting point of a set of perarylphosphonium and sulfonium ionic liquids: the void density method, the hysteresis method, and the solid-liquid interface-based (SLIB) method. Each of these methods requires prior knowledge of the crystal structure, which was obtained experimentally from X-Ray scattering. Furthermore, the experimental melting points were also obtained using differential scanning calorimetry, allowing us to compare these melting points with melting point predictions from each method. Once a model provides an adequate prediction of the melting point, the molecular interactions provided by that model are further studied to understand the molecular-level causes of melting point depression in these compounds. Understanding the molecular interactions of a complex ionic compound will assist in generating new ILs and altering newly formed complex ionic compounds.

title: Carbon Monoxide in Electronic Cigarette Effluent
abstract: The electronic cigarette market has an estimated market value of over $10 billion dollars (2018). While some e-cigarette users are former smokers trying to quit, many youth report e-cigarettes being their only source of nicotine. E-cigarettes are still relatively new devices and their design continues to evolve rapidly. There are many different types of electronic cigarettes on the market, ranging from miniature disposable electronic cigarettes to Advanced Personal Vaporizers (APVs). Some modern e-cigarettes offer customizable temperature/power levels as well. Research on the health effects of these devices is still emerging. However, e-cigarette effluent has been shown to contain formaldehyde, other aldehydes and ketones, other carbonyl compounds, reactive oxygen species and chloropropanols, volatile PAHs and aluminum. It has now been shown, using diode laser absorption spectroscopy, that e-cigarette effluent also contains carbon monoxide (CO). The concentration of CO produced varies as a function of the power of the e-cigarette and the flavor of the e-liquid heated. The CO concentrations ranged from 0 ppm to more than 180 ppm at a high power. CO is a well-known toxicant which when inhaled at high concentration over long periods can lead to death. Short duration exposures are not as well characterized but have shown deleterious health effects.

title: Understanding the Relationship between Engineering Identity and Academic Motivation
abstract: The primary goal in this research is to explore the connection between motivation and identity within undergraduate engineering students. Uncovering the relationship between these two constructs has the potential to inform techniques that encourage academic motivation. In turn, this could encourage a greater correlation between identity and engineering identity. Previous work shows that having a greater intersection between one’s career identity and other identities (i.e., social, demographic, etc.) increases motivation. We hypothesize that this could translate into an academic setting, in which academic motivation is more prevalent among those who have a secure sense of engineering identity. In the end, we believe this will correlate to overall higher success. The method used in this study involves analyzing an individual’s previous responses to failure as a measure of a student’s motivational behavior and comparing this measure to the strength of their engineering identity. The sample population consists of upperclassmen aeronautic and astronautic engineering students. Engineering identity is measured via an instrument created by Dr. Allison Godwin of Purdue University, West Lafayette. The instrument centers on uncovering how strongly students feel they identify as engineers, within categories of recognition, interest, and competence. This study also uses the critical incident technique. Students are asked to reflect upon a time where they successfully and unsuccessfully recovered from an academic or professional failure (the critical incident). Failure is a sensitive subject that provokes strong reactions within people, some greater than others. Thus, in analyzing these reactions, we can gain insight into different patterns of coping mechanisms and determine what patterns hinder or help motivational growth. We are interested specifically in the disciplinary distinction between astronautic and aeronautic engineering students. The subject population in this study is drawn from an upper-level systems dynamics course required for both majors. For students on the astronautic track, it serves as an integral part of their curriculum, while students on the aeronautic track take the course for a greater perspective. In analyzing the difference between majors within the same course, we demonstrate how the intersection between course content and major identity play in subsequent motivation to succeed in the class. This study aims to give educators greater insight into student behavior so they can adjust their teaching techniques to optimize student motivation or encourage greater identity correlation. In future work, we will continue to work through what exactly defines identity, manipulating certain variables to greater understand relationships.

title: Seek and You Shall Find: Where Do Faculty Obtain and Engage with Active Learning Resources
abstract: Different types of active learning are commonly used within classrooms throughout primary and sometimes secondary schools, but upon reaching college classrooms active learning is still gaining traction. The use of active learning techniques can provide an energetic learning environment and has been shown to have a positive effect on student learning. Kinesthetic learning is a branch of active learning that actively and physically engages students with the material being taught through physical movement and/or exercises. Kinesthetic learning specifically moves students around the classroom instead of the traditional sitting for a 50 to 80 minute lecture. Some examples would be rotating stations around the classroom, acting out a process, or students drawing out a process or problem on the board. Kinesthetic and other active learning techniques face many barriers in being adopted in classrooms within the collegiate community. Faculty members can be resistant to changes to the traditional lecture style of teaching, which is possibly connected to a lack of former pedagogical training and awareness of the resources available to support active learning strategies in the classroom. There is also a difficulty in knowing where and how to effectively share materials with other educators when creating active-learning materials. This leads us to the research question: how do faculty members find resources to develop teaching methods for their classrooms? In terms of understanding how to integrate kinesthetic and active learning teaching techniques into college classrooms, information on how faculty members obtain pedagogical skills and methods should be considered. The study conducted seeks to identify where faculty members within engineering disciplines look for resources regarding teaching methods. With this information we can be determine what the best ways are to distribute active learning resources engineering faculty. Data collection through survey and interviews looked at the resources for active learning and how faculty are currently using or are willing to use them. The results lead to information on how to approach developing and disseminating resources to help and improve classroom engagement.

title: 3D Printed Kidney Filters for Hands-on Learning
abstract: In this project, I designed an anatomically correct 3D printed model of a part of the kidney and zoomed in at a more detailed level for a 3D printed component that mimics the filtration of blood by the kidney. I describe the motivations, the models, and their use in hands-on demonstrations for learning science and engineering concepts. The glomerulus, the functional unit of filtration in the kidney, removes waste from the blood while retaining important compounds needed for a healthy body. Glomeruli are a bundle of capillaries surrounded by a capsule and lined with specialized filtration cells. Through physical openings and chemical diffusion, the blood traveling through the capillary is filtered of its waste, which is then excreted as urine. Because the glomerulus is so important in blood filtration, it is a major component in kidney health and important for research studies related to filtration in the body. The glomeruli are found in the thousands in the human kidney but are invisible to the naked eye. With computer aided microscopy, images have been developed and circulated through current literature. However, this data has not yet been used with 3D modeling software to represent the anatomically correct microscopic glomerulus. I used SolidWorks was to model the glomerulus at different spatial scales for demonstration tools. The 3D model of a glomerulus capsule and capillary matrix follows current literature describing the size and volume of an average human glomerulus, which is approximately 200 micrometers in diameter, and considers both artistic renderings and microscopy images currently available. Standard 3D printers and splicing software were used to print each physical model. In this poster, I will justify the development of the 3D glomerulus model highlighting its purpose and use in demonstrations to increase scientific literacy in a variety of venues. I will show the accuracy of my model with respect to current findings on glomeruli size and features. I will also show how a simplified kidney filter was designed and 3D printed for engineering education workshops. Using descriptions and images of glomerular pores, I devised a simple cylindrical filter that when used in tandem with beads representing the various molecules and cells in the blood provides a simple hands-on demonstration of the process of glomerular filtration and how it changes between healthy and diseased conditions.

title: Why Do I Have to KNOW This? Engineering in a Globalized Society
abstract: As society is becoming increasingly globalized, engineers must be able to integrate non-technical factors into their problem-solving and design. This research study investigates whether engineering students, engineering faculty, and professional engineers have similar thinking when it comes to solving problems within a global context. This is aligned with the ABET outcome that students must have “an ability to apply engineering design to produce solutions that meet specified needs with consideration of public health, safety, and welfare, as well as global, cultural, social, environmental, and economic factors,”. This student outcome is referred to as a professional skill. Professional skills were developed as a response to old accreditation standards being too stringent and that they stifled innovation. For engineers, professional skills includes the implicit knowledge of how one’s work impacts a globalized society. At most universities, bringing in global contexts into problem-solving is neglected until students’ senior-year capstone course. This study compares three populations, undergraduate seniors, engineering faculty, and practicing engineers, understanding of the significance of engineering solutions within a global context. Comparing the results from the three populations will provide insight into whether there are discernable differences between the group’s beliefs. Comparing the populations will also provide insight into whether ABET requirements are being met. The results from this study could be used to change how courses or programs are structured to help best prepare students professionally.

title: Effect of Tank Bottom Shapes on N js and Power Dissipation in Stirred Vessels Under Different Baffling Configurations
abstract: Mechanically stirred mixing vessels are widely used in the chemical, pharmaceutical, biotechnology, food, and other related industries to homogenize the liquid content of the vessel and any phase dispersed in it, such as finely divided solid particles. The minimum agitation speed, N js , to just suspend finely divided solid particles in the liquid and the power, P , dissipated by the impeller in these systems are two of the most critical parameters for scaling up mixing processes from laboratory scale to industrial scale. In agitated vessels, the degree of solid suspension can be classified into three levels: on-bottom motion, complete off-bottom suspension, and uniform suspension. Enough agitation is important to completely suspend the solids off the vessel bottom. Below this needed agitation, the total surface area of the solid suspended within the liquid is not completely or efficiently utilized. Therefore, it is important to be able to determine the impeller agitation speed, denoted by N js , at which the just suspended state is achieved. Both N js and P (and its non-dimensional value P o) depend on several factors including type of impeller, its diameter, vessel geometry, and the dynamic conditions at which the mixing is operated (agitation speed). Although most correlations available in the literature for N js and P o were obtained at the laboratory scale using flat-bottom vessels, vessels with hemispherical or torispherical bottoms are much more commonly used in industrial applications. Until now, the effect of the shape of the vessel bottom on N js and P o has received little attention in the literature. Therefore, the main objective of this work was to experimentally determine N js and the power dissipation at these measured N js values for different tank bottom shapes using an axial-flow impeller (Lightnin A310). By using a method recently developed in the mixing lab at NJIT to measure N js , it was found that the hemispherical-bottomed tank dissipated about 15% more power than flat-bottomed tank when tested at the same agitation speed. Additionally, it was found that N js was higher in the hemispherical-bottomed tank than in the flat-bottomed tank. Therefore, the power dissipated in hemispherical bottomed to just suspend the particles was determined to be nearly 50% higher than that of the flat-bottomed system. The results obtained here can be expected to be of significant applicability to industrial systems, such as glass-lined vessels, typically used in the pharmaceutical industry.

title: Metrics of Student Success and Problem Difficulty Using Auto-Graded Online Homework
abstract: Online homework and interactive textbooks are becoming more prevalent in university classrooms . Research suggests that students appreciate the immediate feedback as well as being given multiple attempts to earn points for a problem . However, determining the quality of auto-graded problems is still an open question . To develop a metric, o ver 700 questions were evaluated from a second-semester freshman course in Material and Energy Balances. U sing three years of data from over 250 students and more than 100 ,000 problem attempts were analyzed . Pr oblems consist of multiple parts with each part increasing in difficulty. A variety of problem types were used in including mul tiple choice, numerical response , and graph reading. Metrics used to analyze the que stions included number of attempts before a correct answer was given , total attempts , and success rate . Using these quantities , a point system was created to determine the quality and difficulty of problems based on student performance . Additionally, online homework questions were analyzed to correlate student success in the course with completion of the challenge activity questions. S tudents who complet ed more of the challenge activities had better success in the course as measured by final grade. Overall, web-based analytics of student success and attempts - before - correct can quantify the quality of hundreds of auto-graded problems.

title: Analytical Solution of the Heat Transfer Problem for Power Law Non-Newtonian Fluid
abstract: Accurate predictions of velocity profiles for Non-Newtonian fluids has received considerable attention for about half a century. The specific rheology of these type fluids is well known has an impact on the concentration of species and the corresponding temperature profile in the bulk of the system when mass and/or heat transport occur. Significant research effort has been devoted to the analysis of kinematic viscosity and shear rate to characterize and model the deviation from the Newtonian postulate. However, Non-Newtonian behavior not only directly affects shear stress Newtonian viscosity but also transport of heat in its parameters, thermal diffusion and convective film coefficient. This contribution focuses on the analytical solution of the Energy and Navier-Stokes equations for the case of a Non-Newtonian behavior affecting the main transport physicochemical properties. The power law model, Ostwald-de Waele equation, has been adopted for the solution of the momentum equation. A similar power law expression has been use in the modeling and simulation of the energy equation. The solution strategy uses a similarity approach and the principle of recursion to obtain an explicit mathematical function. Furthermore, this study concentrates on the comparison of the numerical solution and the combined similarity-recursion solution to validate the accuracy of this last method and its predictions. A few different geometries have been chosen to further validate the approach and highlight its simplicity. Concluding remarks are presented to highlight the potential applications of this mathematical tool in the design of heat exchangers.

title: Increasing Chemical Engineering K-14 Involvement By Tackling Water Conservation Using Human-Centered Design
abstract: AIChE 2019 Chemical Engineering Division Increasing Chemical Engineering K-14 Involvement by Tackling Water Conservation using Human-Centered Design Anays Hernandez 1 and Sindia Rivera-Jiménez, Ph.D. 2 1 Department of Chemical Engineering, University of Florida and 2 Institute for Excellence in Engineering Education, University of Florida ABSTRACT How much water does the average person use at home per day? The U.S. Geological Survey reports that old showers may use up to 5 gallons of water per minute and water-saving shower heads produce about 2 gallons per minute. The agency recommends that taking a shorter shower using a low-flow showerhead saves lots of water. Even if an individual invests in a low-flow showerhead, they still need to figure for how long they are showering. A water consumption sensor that relatively anyone can install in their shower head can help to solve this problem. In addition, global market research reported that the environmental sensor market was valued at USD 1.22 billion in 2017 and is expected to reach USD 2.19 billion by 2023. The use of sensors in the K-14 classroom has shown to be of significant educational value because they can help address societies problems while integrating many disciplines such as chemistry, physics, mathematics, computer science, engineering, civics, among others. Exposure to the use of sensors to solve real problems can encourage students to follow career paths in Science Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM), particularly for underrepresented communities. The primary objective of this pilot project is to create a water consumption sensor that is easy to use, and cost-effective for the everyday individual. The integrated sensor system uses simple electrical equipment including photo-resistors, light sources, waterproof cabling, Legos, 3D printed parts, and Arduino. Ideally, this work will become an instructional module that can be used to increase the interest of K-14 students into the chemical engineering field by tackling environmental problems using a human-centered design approach where the needs and wants of the user are paramount for the designer.

title: Investigation of Particle Noise Produced By Tip Sonication
abstract: The tip sonication of nanoparticle solutions can create particulates in test tubes resulting in significant data misinterpretation and faulty results for researchers analyzing nanoparticles. The process of tip sonication is implemented by many researchers who work with nanoparticles to disperse particles. This method is fundamentally applied when nanoparticles are synthesized by nanoemulsion techniques. Low retention, plastic microcentrifuge tubes are typically implemented to store particles, however, previous research has discerned contamination following tip sonication in these tubes. The contamination generated by particulate noise from the tube potentially can result in major inaccuracies. We seek to optimize the process of sonication and reduce data misinterpretation through determining conditions which minimize the contamination particulate formation. In these experiments, ultrapure water is tip sonicated using a Qsonica sonicator and the resulting concentration of contamination particles is measured by nanoparticle tracking analysis. The conditions we have tested include brand of tube used, amplitude and process time. These all impact the concentration of particulate noise produced. Furthermore, several cleaning procedures on the tubes were tested to determine if debris in the tube was the source of the contamination. In addition, we have conducted experimentation to confirm that the particulates we are examining are not bubbles by measuring each sample twice following varying time gaps of ten, twenty and thirty minutes.

title: Lower Extremity Flailing Motions in Response to a Hypothetical Rear-End Vehicular Impact
abstract: Occasionally a victim of a rear-end car crash will experience a lower extremity injury (for example, a patella fracture). One mechanism that has been suggested for such injuries is the result of "flailing" motion (involuntary motions) of the lower extremities that may occur during the impulse phase of the rear end collision. To date, there has been no peer-reviewed literature that indicates that such flailing motions occur that can be causally related to any lower extremity injuries. The purpose of this study is to explore various combinations of driver body geometry (particularly lower extremity dimensions and angles), vehicular interior structure locations (particularly underneath the dash area, steering wheel, and other interior surfaces directly ahead of the driver, and seat positioning. Measurements will be made under two conditions: 1) normal driving position; and 2) after subjects rotate their legs upwards as a simulation of "flailing". First contact point and (if it occurs) 2nd contact points will be documented. Note that a rear end collision is not actually occurring, i.e., only a single stationary unpowered vehicle is employed.

title: Effect of Gamma Irradiation on Antioxidant Activities of Molle ( Schinus molle ) and Guaviduca ( Piper carpunya ) Essential Oils.
abstract: Molle ( Schinus molle ) and guaviduca ( Piper carpunya ) are Ecuadorian endemic species traditionally used as medicinal plants since they have several biologically active components and they are even attributed culinary properties. In this research, the effect of a treatment with gamma radiation on the antioxidant capacity of molle and guaviduca essential oils was evaluated. The essential oils were extracted from dry leaves through hydro-distillation. The irradiation was carried out with a Cobalt-60 source in the raw materials or in the essential oils. The evaluated doses were 10, 15 and 20 kGy. The antioxidant capacity of the oils was determined with the ABTS radical cation and with the DPPH radical methods. In the Schinus molle essential oil irradiated with a dose of 20 kGy before the extraction, the antioxidant capacity increased from 7,71% to 11,07%, while in the Piper carpunya essential oil, the antioxidant activity decreased in all cases due to the irradiation. These results suggest that the ionizing radiations are able to modify the composition of essential oils and modify their properties.

title: Competitive Adsorption and Photocatalytic Degradation of Alizarin Red S and Bromocresol Green Anionic Dyes Using TiO 2 nanoparticles
abstract: Water contamination is a widespread problem that jeopardizing life on earth. The fact that water is capable of dissolving many different substances makes it uniquely vulnerable to pollution. Many human activities are causing direct and indirect water pollution such as landfill, industrial runoff, leaks and spills, mining, etc. Therefore, major steps forward should be taken to treat those water bodies. Cutting edge nanotechnologies are currently invested in order to mitigate water contamination problems and provide environmentally sound solutions. Adsorption and photodegradation using photoactive nanomaterials are considered one of the states of technologies that are used in industrial water purification. This study evaluates the effective photodegradation properties of TiO 2 brookite nanoparticles for the removal of binary aqueous mixtures of the anionic dyes: Alizarin Red S (ARS) and Bromocresol green (BCG). Batch adsorption experiments were conducted to investigate the effect of dyes concentration, contact time, and temperature effect. The adsorption isotherms were fitted for the single adsorption using the models of Langmuir, Freundlich and Sips, while the binary adsorption isotherms were fitted using the Extended-Sips model. The photodegradation experiments for the adsorbed dyes were achieved using UV light irradiation (6 W, λ max = 312 and 365 nm). Overall, post-adsorption photodegradation preliminary results showed high selectivity towards ARS molecules in the presence of BCG molecules. In addition, the adsorption process was spontaneous in nature with endothermic behavior for both anionic dyes. The TiO 2 nanoparticles were successfully regenerated using UV irradiation. Moreover, molecular dynamic computational modeling was performed to understand the molecules optimum coordination, TiO 2 geometry, adsorption selectivity, and binary solution adsorption energies. The outcomes of this study will be showcased and discussed in detail.

title: A Study of the Physical Properties of Plastic Derived Fuel Oil Produced from Waste Plastic
abstract: Plastic waste around the globe has become a massively detrimental issue that can lead to health complications and destruction of the environment. Studies and prior experimentation suggest that thermally decomposing plastic will cause the carbon bonds to break apart and form a fuel oil similar in composition to diesel. Using a low-cost and simple processor called the Trash-to-Tank (3T) processor developed by the University of Kentucky Appropriate Technology and Sustainability (UKATS) Research Team, waste plastic can be converted into fuel, known as Plastic Derived Fuel Oil (PDFO) and sold as a diesel alternative. The 3T processor has been specifically designed to be appropriate for underdeveloped regions where access to sophisticated literature are often lacking. Currently, the UKATS Research Team is conducting a pilot study in Uganda to assess the performance of the 3T process. In order to ensure that the fuel meet all appropriate regulatory requirements for use as a motor vehicle fuel in Uganda, emissions testing has been commissioned from the Ugandan Bureau of Standards. The laboratory results for the PDFO will be presented and compared with traditional number 2 fuel oil. The 3T process has been implemented in Uganda and has the potential to provide a low cost way for rural communities in developing regions to take ownership of the waste plastic problem in their communities. This process is part of the establishment of locally managed decentralized circular economies in underdeveloped regions and further can give women and other people living in poorer regions the ability to become entrepreneurs.

title: Narcotics Consumption Trends at a Southwestern U.S. University Campus in 2018 Tracked By Wastewater-Based Epidemiology
abstract: Current methods measuring the consumption of prescription and illicit drugs are often hampered by innate limitations, which can impact the relevance and robustness of the associated data. Here we applied wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) as a metric to measure trends in the consumption of twelve narcotics within a collegiate setting from January 2018 to May 2018 at a Southwestern U.S. university. Local legislation, put into place because of the opioid crisis, has decreased the number of opioid prescriptions in 2018 by 36% compared to 2016. We hypothesize that per-capita estimates of heroin and fentanyl (illicit alternatives) derived from campus-generated wastewater will be significantly higher (α = 0.05) from the previously sampled academic semester. An initial study, completed for the campus from August 2017 to December 2017 (Fall semester) identified consumption of select narcotics, in units of mg/day/1000 persons in the following order: cocaine (551 ± 49), heroin (474 ± 32), amphetamine (256 ±12), methylphenidate (236 ± 28), MDMA (88 ± 35), oxycodone (80 ± 6), methadone (72 ± 8), alprazolam (60 ± 2), codeine (50 ± 4), and morphine (18 ± 3). The present follow-up study was designed to identify potential changes in the consumption patterns of prescription and illicit drugs as the academic year progresses as well as the occurrence of narcotics not previously investigated at this location. Seven consecutive 24-hour composite raw wastewater samples were collected each month ( n = 70) from two sites that capture nearly 100% of campus-generated wastewater. Samples were extracted using a Dionex 280 AutoTrace solid phase extraction (SPE) system with Oasis Hydrophilic-Lipophilic Balance (HLB) SPE cartridges. Internal standards for target analytes were used to quantify losses during sample processing. Extracted samples were analyzed by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry for the following parent drugs and metabolites: alprazolam, amphetamine, buprenorphine, cocaine, codeine, fentanyl, heroin, MDMA, methadone, methylphenidate, morphine, and oxycodone. Chemical analyses are in progress for the January 2018-May 2018 samples. Forthcoming data will be shared immediately with public health officials to help address the health crisis and to showcase the use of WBE as a tool to directly measure the impact of an implemented public health intervention (i.e., opioid prescription reduction).

title: On-Site Extraction and Electrochemical Analysis of Heavy Metal Pollution in Soil, Plant, Air, and Water Samples
abstract: Heavy metal pollution is a worldwide problem. Within the US these metals are leached into the environment from landfills and from the thousands of mines across numerous mountain ranges (e.g. such as in the infamous Gold King Mine Spill). It is crucial to be able to quantify and identify metals in water, soil, plant, and air to reduce exposures and inform remediation efforts. Currently, the metal testing process often takes days to weeks and requires an equipped laboratory with trained technicians. But imagine if there was a simple integrated device that could not only give you results in minutes but is able to be used on-site. Through a collaboration between Colorado State University and Access Sensor Technologies, we have created a system to do just that. Soil and air filter samples can be immediately placed in a solution capable of extracting metals. Once the extraction is done and adjusted to optimal conditions for the experiment, stripping voltammetry is performed to identify and quantify several different metals including lead and cadmium. In the past, electrochemical techniques have been limited because of the many interferences within the solution, leading to nonsensical results or masking the presence of the metals entirely. However, by modifying the extraction solution and holding at the correct pH we have found many of these interferences disappear, making stripping voltammetry practical for use not only in the lab but also out in the field, where we can determine concentrations down to single part per billion (ppb) levels.

title: Microbial Electrolysis Cell Bio-Degradation of Alkane Compounds
abstract: Alkanes are simple carbon chain molecules that are used in the fuel industry to be combusted to utilize their stored energy. Alkanes are pumped at gas stations across the world for consumers to use, but a majority of gas stations have some amount of alkane contamination that occurs in the surrounding soil that pollutes the environment. In this study, we test a mixed culture of bacteria in a Microbial Electrolysis Cell (MEC) to bioremediate two alkanes, octane and decane, to produce a current to ensure there is activity. The MECs were 120 mL reactor vessels ran in duplicates that contained a graphite anode connected to a Titanium and a stainless steel mesh cathode connected to a 316 stainless steel wire. A voltage of .7 volts was applied to the MECs by a power source and the output voltage from the exoelectrogenic organisms was recorded by Kiethly recording software. We found that a current was produced when the microorganisms found in the soil obtained from a closed gas station near Raleigh that was assumed to have contaminated soil were fed alkanes. The 2 types of alkane reactors produced a current while the control reactor vessels containing acetate, a commonly oxidizable compound, produced no current alluding to the presence of exoelectrogenic microorganisms that could only oxidize alkanes being present in the contaminated soil. These results show promise for bioremediation of alkane polluted soil but it also gives possibility to the potential for co-metabolization to bioremediate other pollutant compounds with similar chemical structures.

title: Ultrasound-Assisted Post-Pyrolysis Magnetization of Biochar without Adsorption Reduction: Effective Removal of Heavy Metals
abstract: Low cost and efficient adsorption of heavy metals from wastewater and thorough removal of adsorbent after water treatment has become the two essential needs. Hence, the main objective of a series of our studies is to develop an advanced acoustic-based method for activation of carbonaceous structures which can be effectively used for adsorption and easily removed from the aqueous solution. Biochar, the solid byproduct of pyrolysis with microporous carbonaceous structure, has been increasingly recognized as an efficient adsorbent for a vast number of pollutants. Magnetization, though eases the separation and reuse of biochar, significantly reduces its adsorption capacity to a comparatively much higher extent.. In this study, a hybrid post-pyrolysis modification was developed which sustained and even significantly increased the adsorption capacity of biochar. The process included i) structural modification of biochar under ultrasound waves, ii) magnetization with magnetite (Fe 3 O 4 ) nanoparticles and iii) functionalization with 3-aminopropyl triethoxysilane (APTES). Low frequency ultrasound irradiation exfoliates and breaks apart the irregular graphite layers of biochar, and creates new/opens the blocked micropores, thus enhancing the biochar’s porosity. On the other hand, APTES stabilizes the nanoparticles on the biochar surface, while it participates in water treatment. Preliminary results showed that acoustic-based magnetic biochar exhibited a much greater ability to remove Ni and Pb, with 124% and 31% higher adsorption compared to raw biochar. This high performance can be attributed to the synergistic effect of ultrasound activation on increasing the porosity and surface area of biochar and its further interaction with amine functionalization using APTES.

title: Rapid Photo-Catalytic Oxidation of Dissolved Manganese with TiO 2
abstract: Manganese(III/IV) (hydr)oxides (hereafter Mn oxides) occur ubiquitously in terrestrial and marine systems, and play crucial roles in natural electron and element cycles. However, the understanding of their occurrence is limited due to the slow oxidation of Mn 2+ (aq) to Mn(IV) which precedes the formation of Mn oxides. Through the photocatalytic process with TiO 2 (the 9 th most abundant compound in the Earth’s crust), we found very fast oxidation of Mn 2+ (aq) to Mn(IV). The reaction rate is even much faster than microbial processes, which has been believed to be the primary mechanism for the oxidation. We studied the oxidation process under a variety of conditions, such as different TiO 2 structures (anatase vs rutile), different solvents (saltwater vs freshwater), and different atmospheric conditions (open air vs nitrogen). These analyses show that the fast photocatalytic oxidation occurs primarily due to direct electron transfer between Mn 2+ (aq) and photo-excited TiO 2 . This understanding will enable us to explain the abundance of natural Mn oxides on rock surfaces. In addition, because the redox process of Cr and Tl, which are newly emerging paleoredox proxie, is significantly governed by Mn oxides, understanding of Mn oxide formation will help to calibrate the redox proxy systems for oxygen evolution on early Earth.

title: Performance Evaluation of Two Cost-Effective Particulate Matter Sensors Under Ambient and Controlled Conditions
abstract: NASA’s Multi-Angle Imager for Aerosols (MAIA) investigation is currently in development for the purpose of studying linkages between different types of airborne particulate matter (PM) and human health. The investigation requires the MAIA satellite instrument to be complemented by networks of surface PM monitors, and will focus on a selected set of major metropolitan areas around the world. In target areas with insufficient surface monitor coverage, the MAIA project will supplement existing reference-grade monitors with cost-effective sensors. To support this objective, we evaluated the performance of PurpleAir-II (PA) and Alphasense OPC-N3 (AS) optical particle counters (OPCs) against size-binned particle counts measured by GRIMM EDM 164, a transportable version of the EPA-approved GRIMM EDM 180, as well as a Differential Mobility Analyzer/Condensation Particle Counter (DMA/CPC). Experiments were performed in indoor and outdoor (i.e., ambient) environments with the PA, AS, and GRIMM, and under controlled laboratory conditions with DMA/CPC in addition to the 3 OPCs. The DMA allows for differentiation of particles based on size, and the CPC grows the particles to larger size for counting. For laboratory evaluations, narrow size distributions of NaCl particles were generated and an airtight aluminum chamber was used to isolate these particles from the external environment. In general, correlations between the low-cost sensors and the GRIMM were a function of particle size and concentration and were generally linear with varying slopes and offsets. In the outdoor environment, PA and AS consistently had R 2 >0.9 for PM 1 and PM 2.5 (particles below 1 µm and 2.5 µm in diameter respectively). PA demonstrated the highest R 2 for most of the PM and counts measurements. In the laboratory, high R 2 was observed in correlations of total counts between GRIMM and DMA/CPC, supporting the use of GRIMM as a reference for size-binned comparisons. For NaCl particles generated with a narrow size distribution (0.5 ± 0.1µm), the OPCs put most of the counts in the smallest size bin (0.3-0.5 µm), but some counts were misclassified to into larger bins. To our knowledge, this study is unique in comparing the response of multiple OPCs to aerosols with controlled narrow size distributions.

title: Point of Entry Water Purification System in Quiché, Guatemala
abstract: The design of a community-wide point of entry water purification system is presented. The system will provide water for up to 600 people in a rural May an community in the Department of Quiche, Guatemala. In the past year, a piping system was installed from a spring located 13 kilometers away. This system relies on gravity to provide water to the homes in the community. The large-scale purifier will be installed at the point of entry to a storage tank. It utilizes solar panels to power the unit and an ultra-violet photoreactor to purify the water and inactivate waterborne pathogens. The design considerations for the purification system included: volumetric flowrate through the system, prefiltration for sediment removal, photovoltaic and battery system for power, and the ability to stop water flow in case of photoreactor failure. The system is designed to exceed a 14 gallon per minute flow rate such that a need for a pump to overcome pressure drop is obviated. When designing the prefiltration, which is necessary for maximum sterilization through the photoreactor, pressure drop measurements were taken to designate which option would best fit the flowrate and pressure drop considerations. The photovoltaic and battery system was designed so that the purification system would be able to run without power from the solar panels for a day and a half. The worst-case scenario for the global horizontal irradiance for the Quiche, Guatemala location was used to calculate how many solar panels and what size battery would be required to do this. A solenoid valve was added to the design to stop the flow of water in case of photoreactor failure. A bypass valve was added prior to the unit, per the communities request, so water could continue to flow in the event of full unit failure. This project was designed and implemented in just under one year. Throughout the year-long journey, one goal was sought after; providing clean water to a developing and well-deserving community in Guatemala as clean water is a human right.

title: Multi-Modal Resins for the Adsorption of Nitroaromatics
abstract: Legacy munition constituents (MCs) including nitroaromatic compounds (TNT, RDX, HMX), along with insensitive high explosives (IHE; NQ, DNAN, NTO), and their degradation products are hazardous molecules that could negatively impact environmental waterways if not removed from wastewater. Although there are remediation techniques in place, new generations of MCs and IHEs are not readily treated. Advanced oxidation processes, such as the Fenton reaction, have been utilized for treatment but are not cost-effective, especially in dilute concentrations, so new technologies are needed. In this work, we propose synthesizing porous, multimodal resins that utilize coulombic interactions, hydrophobic interactions, and hydrogen bonding to improve selectivity for nitroaromatics and overall adsorbent lifetime. Resins synthesized from the monomer glycidyl methacrylate are particularly attractive because they contain reactive epoxy groups which provide a tailorable surface chemistry. Resins are synthesized through suspension polymerization. Properties such as bead size, pore volume, and surface area were manipulated by changing variables such as polymerization temperature, agitation speed, crosslinker ratio, and presence of a porogen. We hypothesize that (1) macroporous resins will provide greater access to binding sites than nanoporous resins and (2) multimodal ligands will exhibit higher selectivity for nitroaromatics than traditional ion-exchange groups. To test the first hypothesis, porous resins are synthesized by including a cyclohexanol and tetradecanol mix in the suspension polymerization reaction. To test the second hypothesis, ligands with multiple modes of binding (i.e. varying degrees of hydrophobicity, H-bond donors, and polarity) were incorporated via epoxide ring opening reactions. Resin functionalization was monitored with Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) by collecting spectra before and after reaction. Resin capacity and binding affinity were studied through equilibrium batch adsorption tests with organic adsorbates phenol, pyridine, picolylamine and benzene. While these are not explosives, they represent adsorbates with varying propensity for H-bonding. Adsorbate concentration in solution is measured by ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy. This work can be extended beyond explosives, because understanding the role of molecular-level interactions in binding affinity will allow for the design of adsorbents that can capture other emerging organic contaminants.

title: Destabilizing Nanosized Biochar
abstract: Biochar has been widely developed as a low-cost and environmental-friendly carbon material for its application in energy, environment, and agriculture. Its applications are largely due to its physiochemical characteristics such as its outstanding porous structure, large surface area, and abundant functional groups which all contribute to its adsorption abilities of contaminants. Recently, a novel method, ball milling has been investigated to enhance the adsorption abilities of biochar in removing organic and inorganic pollutants from contaminated sources. As a new type of engineered biochar, ball-milled biochar (BMB) presents outstanding porous structure, larger surface area, and more abundant functional groups than pristine biochar. Due to its nanosized structure, however, BMB also displays increasing stability and suspension in aqueous environments, which hinders its separation in regard to regeneration and waste disposal. The goal of this research is to investigate to what extent conventional coagulation and flocculation methods could effectively destabilize BMB from aqueous solutions.

title: Study of How the Concentration of Ozone and α-Pinene Precursor Gasses Affect the Hygroscopicity of the Resultant Secondary Organic Aerosol Particles
abstract: Cloud-related phenomena are the largest source of uncertainty in climate models. Thus, many researchers are investigating how various particles interact with water (their hygroscopicity) to form clouds in order to improve these climate models. While the interactions of some chemical species, specifically inorganic salts such as sodium chloride or ammonium sulfate, are well understood, other chemical species are less well understood. One class of particles, called secondary organic aerosols (SOA) which forms from the reactions of gasses in the atmosphere, fall into this class of poorly understood interactions. The reaction of alpha-pinene with ozone to form aerosol particles is a suitable model as both gases are abundant in the atmosphere. Alpha-pinene is a biogenic species that is emitted in by vegetation, while ozone, an inorganic molecule, has both natural and anthropogenic origins. Various methods have already been used by different research groups to investigate the hygroscopicity of the SOA model. However, due to a lack of standardized experimental set-up, comparing results is difficult. To relieve ambiguity, our research group established and used a standardized procedure to explore the effect of different initial concentrations of alpha-pinene and ozone on hygroscopicity.

title: Economic Analysis of Waste-to-Energy Technologies for Urban and Rural Areas
abstract: The average amount of waste generated in the United States is 4.4 lbs/day/person, and the majority is landfilled. The energy contained in these wastes presents an opportunity for renewable energy production. Renewable energy production methods that are more environmentally friendly are needed. Therefore, it is crucial to implement waste to energy technologies to reduce landfilling and minimize environmental impact. Municipal Solid Waste can undergo processes like Anaerobic Digestion (AD), Incineration or Gasification to produce biogas or syngas. Harmful gases produced in landfill can also be used as an energy source. These gases can be upgraded to be used in energy recovery methods like combined heat and power units (CHP), Fischer-Tropsch Synthesis (FTS) for the production of liquid fuels, or the production of Compressed Natural Gas (CNG). All of these technologies are new and minimal data has been reported for their operation. A limitation encountered when trying to implement/build one of these plants is that there is no set tool that compiles the techno-economic and environmental data of existing plants and can provide fast cost estimation for the development of these projects. The goal of this research is to create a software tool based in Excel to assist decision makers such as municipalities and waste management companies. Using this tool, the user is able to select the technology desired: AD, Gasification or Landfilling, as well as the energy recovery method: CHP, liquid fuel or CNG production. The user will also provide the feedstock type (Municipal Solid Waste, Food Waste, Animal Manure, Farm Waste), feed properties and plant capacity. The software tool is set to provide the user with the capital and operational cost requirements and energy profits from the process. Additionally, Carbon balances, biogas production rate and its composition are calculated. The calculator also includes the cost of biogas purification based on the purity requirements for each energy recovery technique. The use of the tool is illustrated using a base case AD plant that generates biogas used to produce liquid fuels via FTS. The plant processes 60,000 dry tons/year of MSW with a 30% moisture content. Using the calculator, the capital cost of the entire system is $17.0 MM and the total operational expenses are $4.46 MM /year. The revenue from tipping fees and liquid fuel sales are $8.6 MM/year. The software tool provides the user with the ability to compare and contrast alternative waste-to-energy options and incentivize building these plants.

title: Oxidation of Reactive Blue 4 through the Use of a Heterogeneous Fenton Catalyst
abstract: Organic aqueous dyes are commonly found in the wastewater of textile companies. Unfortunately, the treatment of these chemicals tends to be complicated, due to their natural resistance to degradation, filtration, and centrifugation. For industrial use, it is important to develop a fast, reusable, and green method to treat and degrade these organic dyes. Therefore, we chose to make use of a Fenton catalytic pathway in the form of Fe 3+ ions. Loading these iron ions on a mesoporous structure, such as SBA-15, was explored to find a way to make the Fenton catalyst more reusable in industry. In other words, to turn a homogeneous catalyst into a heterogeneous catalyst. The heterogeneous catalyst will theoretically be able to retain more of the iron ions than the homogeneous ions after filtration, while still providing active sites for the Fenton pathway. It was found that the iron loaded SBA-15 worked better at oxidizing the reactive blue 4 dye, around 70% oxidation, than just the reagents without the catalyst; however, the experiments ran into complications when an unexpected product was formed within the reaction chamber. With this unexpected product in play, more research will be needed to increase the efficacy of the catalyst as it failed to match up to the homogeneous catalyst.

title: Conceptual Design of Glycol Recovery Method for the Treatment and Disposal of De-Icing Fluid Run-Off and Stormwater Management at Vancouver International Airport
abstract: During the winter months, Vancouver International Airport (YVR) performs de-icing operations during which aircrafts are sprayed with de-icing fluids containing ethylene glycol. The wastewater generated from this process contains ethylene glycol, a component of de-icing fluid, and consequently has a high biochemical oxygen demand (BOD). This wastewater is harmful if it is released into the environment untreated, as high BOD levels reduce the dissolved oxygen (DO) levels and adversely affects the ecosystem. YVR currently implements a periodic offsite disposal system, in which the spent de-icing fluid is collected and sent to Annacis Island Wastewater Treatment plant for further treatment. In addition, the airport’s stormwater runoff periodically exceeds the Canadian Glycol guideline, which mandates that the glycol runoff must not exceed 100 mg/L. The purpose of this project is to present a conceptual design option for the treatment, transport, and disposal of de-icing fluid run-off and management of stormwater runoff. This project analyzes alternative options to YVR’s current waste management method of offsite disposal, with a focus on methods of recovering glycol from spent de-icing fluid. The solution meets environmental regulations, current and future capacity until the year 2050, and manages stormwater run-off outside of de-icing periods. The effects of climate change, airport expansion plans, and flow and loads are taken into to account. A thorough economic study is performed to ensure that the solution is a feasible alternative to YVR’s current operations. The system that is determined to be the most optimal path forward consists of recovering the spent de-icing fluid onsite by utilizing an electric heater and mechanical vapor recompression system, as well as selling the recovered product to a third-party glycol supplier.

title: Characterizing Microplastic Degradation in Simulated Marine Environments
abstract: As more plastic materials accumulate in the ocean, there is a growing concern for their impacts on marine ecology and human beings. This study focuses on establishing characterization methods to investigate the potentially hazardous degradation products of plastics found floating on the ocean surface. Unprocessed plastic pellets (polyethylene, polypropylene, and polystyrene) and consumer drinking straw pieces (non-biodegradable straws and compostable straws) were placed in simulated seawater and examined under different weathering conditions. The effects of ultraviolet light and physical mixing on the rate of degradation using scanning electron imaging was performed to visualize surface degradation. The mass balance of the pellets before and after the degradation process was also analyzed to confirm the scale of degradation. A GCMS protocol is proposed to identify organic degradation species by extracting them from salt water to hexane to confirm the presence and identity of organic degradation byproducts.

title: Study of the Degradation of Chlorinated Pesticides Atrazine and 2,4-D By Continuous System Ozonation
abstract: Atrazine and 2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic Acid (2,4-D) are chlorinated pesticides used for weed control in corn and sugarcane crops; Its presence in water can cause an environmental problem and damage to human health. In Ecuador, the presence of these compounds or their treatment in wastewater has not been investigated, but it is known that the treatments are not specific for their degradation, because these molecules are relatively stable. The project included the study of treatment of synthetic effluents containing atrazine and 2,4-D, through advanced oxidation processes. A continuous ozonification reactor was designed and built with a longitudinal diffuser consisting of two concentric cylinders. The outer cylinder of PVC, 8 mm in diameter and 200 cm in length will be divided into four sections of 50 cm by means of valves for the collection of samples. The ozone diffusion system consists on a silicone cylinder with a diameter equal to 4 mm, with holes of 0.5 mm in diameter to bubble the ozone along the reactor. The effluent entered the reactor with a peristaltic pump and ozone was supplied at rate of 0.84 mg/s through a “PHILAQUA” ozone generator. Atrazine solutions 1.53x10-4 M (33.0 mg / L) and 2.4 D 1.53x10-4 M (33.8 mg / L) were prepared, which were treated in “Batch” and continuous system at different pH values. In continuous system, degradation of atrazine equal to 53.8% was reached at pH 11, and 77.3% of degraded value was mineralized. 250 mL of Atrazine solution were treated in the "Batch" system, in 285.7 s it was affected by the same degradation as in the continuous system and 240.86 mg of Ozone was used. In the continuous system a degradation of 2,4-D equal to 54.4% is detected at pH 11, and 45% of degraded value was mineralized. 250 mL of 2,4-D solution were treated in the "Batch" system and in 424.33 s it was affected by the same degradation as in the continuous system and 357.7 mg of ozone was used. Therefore, continuous system was 2.28 times more efficient than "Batch" system for the treatment of Atrazine and 3.38 times more efficient for the treatment of 2,4-D.

title: Sub-Surface Flow Engineered Wetland Design for Treatment and Disposal of Spent Aircraft De-Icing Fluid at Vancouver International Airport
abstract: Vancouver International Airport (YVR) airside operations de-ice aircraft during winter and utilize an offsite disposal system to manage the spent de-icing fluid and storm-water runoff. The aircraft de-icing fluid (ADF) contains ethylene glycol which is collected on the de-icing pad and conveyed to a ten million litre lagoon and is then transported to the Annacis Island Wastewater Treatment Plant for further treatment. Without being adequately treated, the de-icing fluid and storm-water run-off result in wastewater being generated with a high biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and is toxic if released into the environment. The purpose of this project is to design and analyze biological treatment as an alternative to offsite disposal of the ADF and present the treatment, conveyance and disposal of fluid and present an economic and environmental justification to support the implementation of the solution. The design process involves examining several biological treatment options to meet design constraints of not interfering with airside operations, maximizing the use of existing assets when possible, not attracting wildlife and can be built within the confines of the airside boundaries. A hydraulic feasibility study, life cycle analysis and economic study are conducted to determine the most ideal and viable option. The biological treatment chosen and designed is an artificially aerated engineered wetland system which can withstand current and future capacity until the year 2050, meets all municipal provincial and federal regulatory requirements and can store storm-water runoff outside the de-icing periods.

title: Electrospun Polymer-Based Visible Colorimetric Sensor for Selective and Sensitive on-Site Determination of Polycyclic Aromatics Hydrocarbons in Aquatic Ecosystems
abstract: Water is an integral part of our society. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) resulting from oil spills and industry pollution are of particular concern to the Gulf Coast area, as these areas represent a critical nexus of food-energy-water for the region and the greater United States. Through this work an electrospun polymer-based PAH-in-water sensor will be devised. This will provide insight into the underlying phenomena of the advanced preconcentration and sensing methods used. Here, silica nanofibers with a formaldehyde detection chemistry were used to detect PAHs down to the ppb-scale using a small sample (~10 mL) wihtout the need for analytical equipment. This allows water samples to be tested on-site and in real time. The research has addressed the advanced material and interfacial challenges of the polymer-based sensors and the operational challenges of sensors for aquatic ecosystem monitoring. This work is applicable to a wide array of water sensing functionalities and integrations.

title: Ionic Strength Effects on Flocculation Performance in Taylor-Couette Flow
abstract: The removal of flocs, which are aggregates consisting of solid particulate, from source water is an essential part of the drinking water treatment process. To improve flocculation, salt can be added to increase the solution ionic strength. This creates a charge screening effect, which allows for aggregation of particulate. However, increasing the salt concentration would increase the load on reverse osmosis filters down the line, which is cost prohibitive. The addition of long-chained, charged polymer flocculants makes the flocculation possible without need for excess salt. Flocculation in a treatment tank is subject to a variety of hydrodynamic flow states, and isolating how they affect flocculation is difficult. A Taylor-Couette (TC) cell, which consists of two concentric cylinders where the gap between the cylinders can be filled with fluid, can generate precisely defined flow states at specific rotational speeds. The Dutcher group has built a TC cell with radial injection capabilities from the inner cylinder, therefore flocculation can be captured via image analysis from the start of the process. This TC cell will be used to study how different concentrations of NaCl impact flow dynamics and floc size, growth rate, and configuration.

title: Aqueous Film-Forming Foams Containing per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances and Their Precursors: Characterization and Treatment Options
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are chemical compounds that have been used in numerous industries, commercial applications, and extensively in aqueous film-forming foams (AFFF) for fire-fighting activities. They are environmentally persistent compounds and reported to cause adverse effects on human health. According to the USEPA, currently available industrial formulations of AFFF should be free from long-chain perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAAs) which are the most commonly found PFAS in the environment and thought to be the most problematic. This project was centered on characterizing three industrially formulated and currently available AFFF samples to determine whether PFAAs can be destroyed by oxidizing the PFAS precursors using various advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) and utilizing plasma treatment for the oxidized samples. Preliminary measurements of 12 PFAA and 10 precursors with an LC-MS/MS have shown high concentrations of short-chained PFAA, traces of long-chain PFAA, and a significant amount of PFAS precursors. The 6:2 fluorotelomer sulfonate (6:2 FTS) was present at high concentrations in the three samples. Preliminary treatment experiments were performed by adjusting the dosage of the oxidation treatments in diluted AFFF samples. Once the optimization of the oxidation treatments is completed, efforts towards oxidizing PFAA for complete treatment of AFFF with preliminary plasma treatments will be realized. title: Removal of Antibiotic-Resistant Bacteria in Synthetic Stormwater Via Biochar Columns
abstract: Water is one of the world’s most valued commodities, and antibiotic-resistant bacteria are one of the emerging pollutants of concern. Stormwater runoff picks up pollutants such as chemicals, bacteria, and sediment as it runs over impervious surfaces and into waterbodies. The aim of this project is to test the use of biochar columns as an effective and inexpensive form of stormwater treatment. Biochar is biomass that has undergone pyrolysis. It serves as an adsorbent for contaminants in water including antibiotic - resistant bacteria. It is commonly used in land applications as a soil amendment, but there are concerns as to how long biochar is effective and what occurs once the biochar is saturated. Three infiltration columns will be tested; one containing biochar, one with soil and biochar mixed in a ratio typically seen in a soil amendment, and one with soil. Due to the unpredictability of stormwater, semi-natural stormwater will be synthesized by inoculating stormwater collected from the OSU-Benton County Green Stormwater Infrastructure Research Facility with several E. coli strains. Using culture-based methods, E. coli in the synthetic stormwater will be quantified before and after treatment through columns in triplicates. The ability of the columns to both remove and retain an adequate concentration of E. coli will be analyzed to determine the best step for future use of biochar.
