title: Modeling UV-Visible Absorbance Spectra of Multiple-Component Carbonyl-Containing Aqueous Aerosol Mimics
abstract: Proper characterization of atmospheric brown carbon (BrC), its formation, and its absorbance effects are critical to understating the aggregate effect that these materials have on overall aerosol climate forcing. Since a vast of chromophoric compounds can be produced from a single dicarbonyl/ammonium pairs, it is impractical to identify every specific chromophoric species that comprises an aerosol's overall absorbance spectrum as a reaction system ages. Therefore, we present an alternative method of representing UV-visible absorbance spectra as a composite of multiple, dynamic spectral line shapes. Previous work demonstrated that a model with four fitted Gaussian curves with magnitude following first-order kinetics achieves accuracy within 66% in the 200-350 nm range to track the absorbance behavior of single carbonyl/ammonium reaction systems (methylglyoxal and glyoxal) with different reagents concentrations and aging times. This research aims to verify the validity of this model on a complex carbonyl mixture (methylglyoxal and glyoxal)/ammonium reaction system. Absorbance data for varying concentrations of methylglyoxal and glyoxal in ammonium sulfate solutions were measured and modeled. Results were compared to the model gained by directly adding up the model of individual reaction systems. Residual analysis indicated that instead of fix at 220 nm, the peak of one of curve was within the range of 215 to 220 nm. Finally, a new peak was formed at around 225 to 230 nm. Therefore, a new Gaussian curve and the interaction parameters were added to track the result of the interaction between methylglyoxal and glyoxal.

title: Extracting and Detecting Uranyl Species Using Aliquat-PAN Mats and Gold Nanostars
abstract: The ability to detect and specify trace concentrations of uranium in groundwater is crucial to addressing public health concerns associated with uranium in groundwater and restoring adversely impacted lands. Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) detection of trace concentrations of uranium on polymer mats has been previously reported using amidoximated-polyacrylonitrile (AO-PAN) mats and carboxylated gold nanostars, but a reproducible method of determining uranyl species in aqueous solution is still needed. In this project, we seek to utilize Aliquat 336 polyacrylonitrile (Alq-PAN) mats to isolate the original uranyl species from solution, followed by separation analysis at trace concentrations based on unique vibrational frequencies in SERS spectra with gold nanostars. To observe how efficiently Alq-PAN mats isolate and uptake negatively-charged uranyl species, we varied the uranyl-to-oxalate concentration ratios (5:50, 5:100, 5:300) of the aqueous solution and incubated Alq-PAN mats within the aqueous solution. We hypothesize that increasing the number of oxalate ligands, or increasing the uranyl-to-oxalate concentration ratio, will increase the number of negatively-charged uranyl-oxalate species in solution, thus promoting uranyl uptake and SERS detection. Understanding the interaction between Aliquat and uranyl-oxalate complexes will allow us to extend the speciation analysis to other aqueous samples with different negatively-charged uranyl species, such as uranyl-carbonate or uranyl-phosphate.

title: Open Borehole Cross-Contamination: A Unique Opportunity to Evaluate Natural Attenuation of Mixed Organic Contaminants in a Sedimentary Rock Aquifer System
abstract: At a site in Wisconsin, organic chemicals were released into the subsurface resulting in the formation of a persistent, dense non-aqueous phase liquid (DNAPL) source between 46 and 55 m below ground surface (bgs) in a fractured sandstone. Since 2003, researchers have applied various hydrogeological measurement and modeling techniques to characterize the flow system, contaminant mass, and phase distributions. In July 2017, three holes were continuously cored to 100 m bgs, downgradient of the source zone (MP-23D, MP-24D, and MP-25D). The cores were geologically logged and sampled (about 5 per 1.5 m) for contaminant analyses by removing a puck from the core, crushing it in a hydraulic press, and placing about 15 g of the rock into a pre-prepared vial of high purity methanol for contaminant extraction. The rock core results quantify the total (i.e., dissolved, sorbed, NAPL) contaminant mass in the rock matrix pore space. Then the coreholes were logged using geophysical and hydrophysical methods in the open and FLUTe™ sealed boreholes. Prior to multilevel system (MLS) installation, the holes were sealed with FLUTe™ liners unless open hole measurements were being made. Each borehole was instrumented with high resolution (20 monitoring intervals over 40 m) Westbay® MLS in November 2017 and used to sample groundwater in June 2018 and 2019. These MLS samples represent the water and contaminant mass in the fractures. The rock core was expected to have high, quantifiable results through 55 m bgs. Therefore, permanent casings were set at 60 m bgs before proceeding with coring. The rock core data showed consistent, high concentrations through 62 m bgs and sporadic quantifiable concentrations separated by non-detects were identified to 83 m bgs. In contrast, high, quantifiable concentrations were observed from 60–98 m bgs in groundwater samples from all three MLS. The discrepancy between the rock core and MLS groundwater data suggests the boreholes became cross-connected during open hole conditions. Repeat groundwater sampling in the MLSs show concentration declines in the deepest portion of all three holes and drastic compositional changes for all MP-25D ports. The cross contamination of these boreholes provides an opportunity to study natural attenuation of these chemicals in a sedimentary rock aquifer system with baseline conditions obtained from rock core VOC data. Future work will consist of comparing the depth discrete groundwater concentration trends to hydrophysical data quantifying active flow regions in each hole and analyzing mechanisms and rates of the natural attenuation.

title: Environmental Fate and Transformation of Dichloroacetamide Herbicide Safeners
abstract: Dichloroacetamide safeners are a class of agrochemicals co-applied in large scale with chloroacetamide herbicides to protect crops from herbicide toxicity. Although all four dichloroacetamide species have been detected in Midwestern surface waters, safeners are currently regulated as “inert” constituents under the U.S Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act, and as such, have received meager attention in the peer-reviewed literature. Recent studies suggest that some dichloroacetamide safeners are reactive in aquatic systems and can yield products with increased bioactivity which may pose risks to human and environmental health. To evaluate the fate and transformation of dichloroacetamide safeners, we measured timescales (i.e. half-lives, sorption rates) for predicting safener persistence, determined the effects of water chemistry (i.e. pH, DOC) on the rate and extent of hydrolysis and sorption processes, and quantified sorption parameters for active herbicide co-formulants and mixtures. We found that most dichloroacetamide safeners undergo both acid-catalyzed and base-catalyzed hydrolysis, and we identified two hydrolysis products for benoxacor, the most widely-used dichloroacetamide safener. Sorption studies revealed limited uptake of safeners and herbicide co-formulants, with more sorption to soil with a high organic carbon content. In general, dichloroacetamide safeners demonstrated reduced uptake onto soil compared to their chloroacetamide herbicide co-formulants.

title: Investigation of Presence and Role of Polyphosphate Accumulating Organisms (PAOs) in Lake and Sediment
abstract: The international community faces an imminent global phosphorus crisis. There exists a growing need for phosphate as fertilizer for agricultural food production, but large amounts of phosphate are wasted and end up polluting water resources. Polyphosphate accumulating organisms (PAOs) are known to uptake phosphorus under aerobic conditions and can store polyphosphate. When switched to anaerobic conditions, PAOs will then release phosphate and obtain energy through the cleavage of polyphosphate. The Gu Research Group in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at Cornell University partnered with the Cornell Biological Field Station to examine the presence and abundance of polyphosphate and PAOs in Oneida Lake. A series of core sediment samples were collected weekly over a one-month period and transported to Cornell University for preparation and subsequent analysis using Raman spectroscopy, flow cytometry, and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. The bacteria were isolated from sediment samples using density and mechanical separation methods. Both flow cytometry and subsequent analysis using Raman showed that polyphosphate-containing cells are present in the sediment and they appeared to correlate with DO levels at the surface of the sediment. Further experiments, such as colorimetric analysis, ion chromatography, and NMR, need to be conducted to confirm the absolute concentration of polyphosphate in the sediment samples. The findings from this study can benefit the search for PAOs to mitigate the global phosphorus crisis.

title: Analyzing the Effects of Surface Energy on Algae with Specialized Attachment Mechanisms in Static and Flow Environments
abstract: The goal of this research is to observe the effects of surface energy on the attachment of algae with specialized attachment mechanisms to substrata in stationary environments and small, controlled flow environments. The substrate materials tested are glass and polylactic acid (PLA). Reactor channels were 3D-printed from PLA filament and a standard glass microscope slide and pressed PLA were used as the substrates for attachment. The algae species in focus for this experiment are two types of filamentous green algae, Oedogonium and Stigeoclonium. Oedogonium is known to have root-like structures, called holdfasts, and mucilage basal pads as a specialized attachment mechanism. Stigeoclonium is a freshwater algae that has a specialized “star-like” attachment mechanism that is known as basal rhizoids. In nature, multiple algae types grow together on rocks and surfaces, but the factors affecting algal attachment are not fully understood. Different types of algae are preferred for different commercial applications, such as pollutant removal, nutrient supplements, and biofuel production. The economic viability of algae cultivation could be improved if the details governing algal attachment were better understood.

title: Study of a Treatment System Based on a Biofilter Using " Eisenia Foetide " Worms, for the Treatment of Effluents from a Slaughter Company
abstract: This study is based on the evaluation of a wastewater treatment system of a slaughtering industry based on a vermifilter built with low-cost recyclable material using Eisenia foetide worms as degrading organisms with a concentration of 200 units /m 2 , the analyzed effluent has high concentrations of contaminants such as BOD with 1401 mg/L, a COD of 3642 mg/L, total suspended solids 1437 mg/L and oils and fats of 1313 mg/L. For this support , the constants of the Schulze equation that relates the residence time to the height of the filter were determined , the average dimensional constants obtained were n=1,0940 and C = 0.0305. Six 0,27 m 2 filters were built and kinetics were analyzed with residence times of 4, 8, 14, 17, 21 and 24 h with a hydraulic load of 3 L/ day . For this effluent the vermifilter presented a first-order degradation kinetics with a constant k=0.1078 h -1 . Wood chips were used as a filter bed due to this material is a waste in the local timber industry and has a low cost . In addition , recycled material was used for the construction of vermifilters which allows the system to be low cost of implementation and high duration . These systems have several advantages such as the formation of high quality solid fertilizer as a by-product and low energy consumption . The evaluation of this system will allow the design of a wastewater treatment plant for the total flow of the company .

title: Wastewater Treatment of Urea-Formaldehyde Resins Reaction By Heterogeneous Fenton with Goethite and Coupled By Distillation
abstract: In this study, degradability of contaminants present in effluents from urea-formaldehyde reaction resin was investigated. The degradation process consisted in distillation combined with Fenton Heterogeneous. In this research, temperature, distillation time, pH, reaction time, and catalyst dosages were varied in order to obtain the best set of conditions. This set was stablished to be 100°C, 2h for distillation, pH of 3,8; goethite and/or goethite impregnated in silice sand concentration equal to 3 g/L. Fenton Heterogenous process was performed at local conditions of pressure and temperature, and stirring speed was 250 rpm. Degradation was measured with chemical oxygen demand (COD). For distillation without Fenton Heterogeneous, the COD was found to be 71,01%. For the process with Fenton Heterogeneous after distillation, this value was 57,61%. The COD values were evaluated in conjunction with the reduction of total organic carbon (TOC). For distillation combined with Heterogenous Fenton, the reduction in TOC was about 49,77% more. Something important to mention, separation time of water and goethite impregnated in silica sand is much shorter than separation time of water and just goethite. This investigation demonstrated that distillation combined with Fenton Heterogenous process has a potential for efficient mineralization of waste from of urea-formaldehyde resins production.

title: Greenhouse Studies for Phytoremediation of Soil at Legacy Uranium Mining Site
abstract: Historical mining practices have contributed to long term environmental impacts to soil and water and may pose a risk to public health if not managed appropriately. The focus of this study is to phytoremediate soil and water with elevated levels of radionuclides, including radium and uranium, at a legacy uranium mine in northern New Mexico. Uranium present is undergoing radioactive decay, producing radium as one of decay products at levels that require remediation before the land can be returned to other uses. Part of a proposed closed-loop system to remediate the water and soil affected involves using plants to remove uranium and radium from the soil. Here, greenhouse studies are being conducted to determine which plants are most effective for uptake of the heavy metals. In the first greenhouse study (summer 2019), spring canola (Brassica napus var. L140), safflower (Carthamus tinctorius var PI544006), guar (Cyamopsis tetragonoloba var. Kinman), carinata (Brassica carinata0, confectionary sunflower (Helianthus annus var. Red River 2215), and several native grass species were germinated and placed in pots containing contaminated soil collected from the legacy mine site. Of these plants, the confectionary sunflower, guar, spring canola, and carinata grew sufficient biomass for analysis. One challenge noted was the heavy texture of the soil, which limited root penetration of the transplanted seedlings into the contaminated soil and which affected plant-available water. Soil properties, and nutrient and metal levels, were measured using inductively-coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), gamma spectroscopy, and liquid scintillation counting before transplanting and after harvest. For the second greenhouse study (winter 2019-2020), winter canola (Brassica napus) and hemp (Cannabis sativa) will be added to the studied species, a new contaminated soil sample with lighter texture will be used in the pots, and plants will be directly seeded. Special attention will be paid to the soil moisture content. Results from the greenhouse studies will be used to inform design of an on-site study at the legacy mine site.

title: Scale-up of Moringa Coated Sand Filters
abstract: Clean drinking water is a global issue, affecting more than 844 million people around the world. The proposed project is to scale-up and redesign a Moringa seed coated sand filter to remove bacteria from wastewater with locally accessible and affordable materials. Moringa seeds contain a cationic protein that can create electrostatic forces between negatively charged microbes, removing the pathogens present in the water. For the purpose of this study, the lab-scale glass columns used for the filters were replaced by PVC pipes, using a binary mixture of collector size and increasing the column diameter and flow rate according to the Clean Bed Filtration Model to obtain the EPA standard approved removal. To prove the functionality of the filters, fluorescent E. coli bacteria was first utilized to quantify the experimental removal. It was then noted that when treating water spiked with E. coli and TOC, the organic matter (TOC) competes with the bacteria for protein sites, impeding the proper removal. To address this problem, an activated carbon pre-filter was implemented. The results showed that, when this pre-filter is applied, the TOC sticks to the activated carbon particles, allowing the f-sand filter to function properly and remove bacteria above the EPA standard approved removal.

title: Exploration of the Efficiency of Surfactant Extraction from High Internal Phase Emulsions
abstract: Clean water and clean air filtration are essential for environmental sustainability, in which there is a need to provide efficient ways to process both fluids to help communities have healthy lifestyles. One component that can improve the filtration is the use of foams. Foams are porous substances that have a combination of a continuous phase and an internal (or dispersed) phase. Pores of the foams consist of the dispersed phase of the foam formed in conjunction with surfactants. Surfactants are substances that lower surface tension between two immiscible phases, which results in a more stable interface between both phases. In more general applications, surfactants are used in conventional products such as soaps and detergents, in which the surfactants help with filtering any unwanted chemicals and compounds. In the emulsification process, the surfactant gets mixed in with the high internal phase emulsions and gets washed off using soxhlet extraction. However, there has not been any studies on the quantity of surfactant that is washed off. This is an issue due to the fact that surfactants will contain unwanted contaminants in which will cause toxicity in water quality. In this project, we investigated the process of polymerization of a water/monomer system, more specifically the step of washing the surfactant off. This step of the process is essential because, in most applications, the surfactant is washed off to decrease in the possibility of contaminates still present and can cause impure products. The parameters that will be tested are (1) how long does it take to wash out the surfactant, (2) what solvent works best to wash out the surfactant as well as to analyze what surfactant we are using (for this experiment we will be using Polysorbate 80, Polysorbate 20, Span 20, and Span 80), and (3) how can we quantify how well the surfactant is washed off. UV-visible spectrometry was in this experiment as it can analyze the absorbance of a solution with light. With this and Beer-Lambert’s law, which states that the absorbance of the compound is directly proportional to the concentration of the solution, we can produce conclusions on the washing off of surfactants and how we can manipulate the step to efficiently provide filtration mechanisms. The resolution before and after the wash of the surfactant can easily be measured and help understand the parameters of this part of the process related to emulsion-based polymerization.

title: Carbon Dioxide Removal and Oxygen Replenishment While Producing Proteins within a Mars Human Space Camp
abstract: NASA plans to have humans living on Mars for long periods of time within the next 20 years. There are many challenges that must be addressed before this vision is realized. Humans within confined cabins, like a Mars planetary surface camp, produce carbon dioxide as they respire and take in the oxygen from within the provided cabin air. The University of Louisiana working in concert with NASA and the Louisiana LASPACE program are researching methods to remove carbon dioxide as it builds up within the cabin air and potentially converting it to oxygen for reuse. Another potential source of carbon dioxide within the cabin is generated during the aerobic biotreatment of wastewaters produced during the support of humans on Mars. Additionally, the team hopes to produce protein from microalgal systems performing the carbon dioxide to oxygen photosynthetic conversion. Two primary methods are under consideration. One involves precipitation of carbon dioxide using sodium hydroxide solutions. The solid-precipitated carbonates produced are fed to chlorella microalgae to yield proteins (non-gas phase transfer of carbon to the algae). The second method is direct sparging of the spent cabin air into the chlorella where the gas-phase carbon dioxide is utilized for autotrophic growth. All cultures are grown in photobioreactors that are irradiated using fiber optics simulated sunlight (initially earth irradiation is tested then simulated Mars sun-irradiated will be tested using specialized lamps). The overall process flow diagram, theory of conversion, simulated yields, and initial results will be presented in the poster.

title: Quantification of Uranium and Radium in Soil and Water Phytoremediation
abstract: Leachates from spent ore piles and mine tailings, and small particles moved by the wind, have enriched uranium and its decay products (radium) in the soil and water near legacy uranium mines in northern New Mexico. To be effective, combined remediation of both soil and water is needed. In this study, algae are being tested for their uptake of radionuclides and heavy metals from groundwater and several species of terrestrial plants are being evaluated for their ability to extract radionuclides from the contaminated soil. Two categories of terrestrial plants have been selected for this study, cellulosic oil-producing. Evaluation of the phytoremediation efforts requires quantification of uranium, radium, and other metals in the water, soil, and produced biomass. Given the low concentrations of the metals and the occasionally small sample sizes, quantification involves multiple strategies. Plants are partitioned into roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and (oil)seeds. Each part is analyzed to help understand the movement and aggregation of radionuclides in plants. The overarching goal is to be able to produce fuels from the plant material that remains uncontaminated while reducing waste volume and preventing further spread of contamination. The analytical techniques being considered are inductively-coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) for heavy metals and higher levels of uranium; high-resolution, dual channel ICP mass spectroscopy (ICP-MS) for low metal concentrations and radium; gamma spectroscopy, and liquid scintillation counting. Most of these analyses require multi-step sample preparation including drying, ashing, acid digestion, filtering, ion exchange chromatography fractionation, and spiking with standards. Here, we present preliminary results about phytoremediation efficiency and the potential for value-added use of the produced biomass.

title: Phosphate Adsorption Using Nitrogen Doped Biochar from Egg Shells and Egg Carton Feedstock
abstract: The project discusses the potential use of biochars produced from waste for phosphate(P) removal. Different series of biochar were produced from different ratios of eggshells and egg cartons to find the optimal ratio of eggshells to egg carton for the adsorption of phosphates. The biochars were produced through pyrolysis of feedstock under a nitrogen gas atmosphere at 750 C. In order to characterize the biochar, the samples were analyzed using TGA, BET surface analysis, CHN, FTIR and pH. Elemental and proximate analysis showed that eggshells have a high concentration of ashes and nitrogen. The pyrolysis decreased the carbon content in the 1:1 shell to carton biochar but increased the nitrogen content. The best variation of biochar produced was an eggshell biochar under nitrogen at 750 C and had a peak adsorption capacity of around 955 mg PO 4 /g of biochar. This was promoted by the basicity of the solution which was measured to be 12. The eggshells promoted chemical adsorption through precipitation. Langmuir isotherms were fitted to all data sets but only ratios with equal or more carton fit the isotherm. The BET analysis showed increased surface area in samples produced from higher levels of egg carton. The mixture of 1:3 shell to carton had a surface area of 241.24 m 2 / g and the eggshell alone had a surface area of 12.82m 2 / g. Eggshell samples had smaller surface area but high adsorption capacity due to presence of Calcium (Ca) that allowed for the formation Ca-P crystals. This project shows that eggshells could be applied as a source of calcium to produce biochar with high phosphate adsorption capacity.

title: Chemical Model of Raritan River Sediment for Lead Sensor System
abstract: In collaboration with the Environmental Science department at Rutgers University and the Center for Advanced Infrastructure and Technology (CAIT) this project seeks to develop a fast-acting sensor system and MINTEQ model program capable of producing a total Pb concentration from “fresh” sediment on the order of minutes. Pb concentrations in various chemical fractions of Raritan River sediment and environmental data was used to optimize a sediment geochemical model in MINTEQ. The MINTEQ geochemical model is used to determine the environmental conditions at various river sites that influence the fractions of lead bound to: dissolved organic matter (DOM), sulfide, carbonates, and hydrated ferrous oxide (HFO), an important fraction in the Raritan River. The MINTEQ model calibrated at a pH of 7.4 generates Pb 2+ fractions of 11.805% bound to DOM, 65.172% bound to sulfide, 0.677% bound to carbonate, and 19.816% bound to HFO similar to those seen in field samples. In a pH sweep of the model from 6.4 to 8.4, the Pb fraction bound to sulfides decreases while the fraction bound to HFO and DOM increased. A Cl sweep from 0.03 to 0.5M, indicates that additional Pb-Cl species form in higher concentrations of Cl with the fractions of each species increasing with Cl. The effect of HFO concentration was tested in a sweep from 0.00036 to 0.00056 g/L increasing the Pb fraction bound to HFO and decreasing the fractions bound to sulfide. These initial results indicate a MINTEQ model can improve our Pb speciation model from laboratory measurements in atypical chemical conditions when it errors significantly from total sediment Pb concentrations and provide data of Pb partitioning from sites not accessible by boat. Our sensor system and geochemical model opens the opportunity for accurate on-site Pb measurements and the potential to measure sediment Pb concentrations of an entire watershed within days. This point-of-use technology has the potential to quickly identify Pb contaminated areas for remediation and augment treatment processes for Pb in polluted sediment.

title: Microbial EPS Impact on Residual Water Saturation in Emulated Soil Micromodels
abstract: Microbial communities are an integral part of soil environmental conditions. Within soil, bacteria contribute to moisture retention by secreting extracellular polysaccharides (EPS). EPS helps regulate moisture retention by reducing water evaporation, in turn promoting plant growth. EPS mitigates water loss at pore-scale by (i) acting as a hydrogel, which will swell during wet conditions and retain moisture in dry conditions, (ii) promoting soil aggregation, resulting in porous microstructures that increase the interparticle capillary forces, and (iii) altering soil surface properties such as hydrophobicity. Studies on moisture retention at bulk scale have few chances to uncover these intricate interactions among microbes, soil and solution systematically. Here, we employed an emulated soil micromodel to examine the mechanisms of moisture retention on EPS collected from Sinorhizobium meliloti cultures and compared them to the drying effects of deionized water, dilute glucose solution, and artificial groundwater (AGW). The results showed that EPS reduce the evaporation rate and promoted residual saturation at equilibrium compared with AGW and DI water within identical physical geometry. Dilute EPS (0.006%) in AGW solution had an average residual saturation of 2.8 ± 2.94% after 16 hours drying. Comparatively, deionized water reached 0% residual saturation after 6 hours drying, artificial groundwater reached 1.6 ± 3.19% saturation after 6.5 hours, and dilute glucose in AGW solution (0.006%) reached 3.6 ± 3.61% saturation after 8 hours. In this study, we confirmed the effect of EPS on moisture retention at pore-scale and provide a platform to understand microbial-mediated moisture retention. Ultimately, we hope this work to aid in implementing sustainable agriculture leading to increased food production and less water usage.
authors: Leslie M. Shor | University of Connecticut

title: E. coli Removal in Moringa-Coated Sand Using Binary Mixtures
abstract: Providing access to clean water is one of the 14 grand challenges on engineering. 1 billion people do not have access to clean drinking water more than 4,000 children under the age of five die daily due to diarrhea diseases linked to drinking unclean water. This study offers moringa oleifera seed coated sand solution as an option for sustainable water treatment. The moringa seed is readily available in countries that need safe drinking water the most. One tree produces 15,000 seeds in one year and the seeds contains 1% cationic protein allowing it to act as a coating for sand. The charge on the seed attracts to the sand, reversing the charge of the sand surface. Coating very fine sand (106 micron) with moringa seeds removes 100% of E. coli from our lab-scale columns and satisfies the EPA standard. However, the removal decreases significantly with larger sand size and the limited access to this size sand defeats the purpose of our solution. One solution is to mix this small sand with practical sieved sand to produce binary mixtures. Our hypothesis was that this mixture will provide the same hydraulic conductivity and bacterial removal. Our experiments confirmed this hypothesis. The hydraulic conductivity experiments showed that binary mixtures of 40% sieved sand and higher should behave the same as the successful 100% 106-micron columns. The E. coli removal experiments proved this hypothesis correct, showing binary mixtures of 40% and higher have similar removal as 100% 106-micron sand. The next steps in this project include scaling up the column containing the binary mixtures, and using activated carbon to remove organic matter in real water.

title: Depolymerization of Polyethylene Terephthalate Plastics By Ozonolysis
abstract: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is the most abundant of the seven categories of recycled plastics due to its affordability and desirable chemical properties for use in diverse applications such as the ubiquitous containers and synthetic fibers. The improper disposal of plastics contributes to environmental pollution adversely affecting nearly all types of ecosystems. Beyond washing and reusing consumer plastics, chemical or tertiary recycling breaks plastics down into constituent monomers which may be transformed to make new consumer products. However, such techniques are still in the research and development stages. Herein, we investigate a new method that attempts to break down PET using ozone (a powerful oxidant that is also used in water purification and deconstruction lignin, a naturally occurring biopolymer) to decompose the polymers into smaller molecules for reuse. To perform ozonolysis, a solvent that dissolves PET and is itself inert to ozone is essential. Among various solvents [acetic acid, tetrahydrofuran (THF) and trifluoroacetic acid (TFA)] in preliminary studies, TFA demonstrates high PET solubility as well as compatibility with ozone. Bubbling ozone (9.4 mole% in O 2 ) through such a PET solution produces several smaller molecules including terephtalic acid (TPA) as inferred by NMR spectroscopy. These initial results are promising as TPA is a starting material for producing PET plastic. They provide guidance for future research towards making chemical recycling practically viable, thereby improving environmental sustainability.

title: Modulation of Cationic Nanocarrier Properties for Penetration of Blood-Brain-Tumor Barrier and Glioblastoma Treatment
abstract: Glioblastoma multiforme is a Grade IV malignant invasive tumor of the central nervous system that has a 3-5% 2 year survival rate. Treatment is made difficult by the inability of chemotherapeutics to effectively penetrate the blood-brain-tumor-barrier (BBTB), a highly selective interface that only allows the intercapillary transport of small (50-100 nm), lipophilic molecules; these properties are not present in modern chemotherapeutics. Previous research in the Peppas lab has produced pH-responsive polymeric nanocarriers capable of drug complexation and targeted therapeutic delivery. To apply these nanocarriers to glioblastoma treatment, their sizes and surface charges must be controlled at the synthesis stage to fit the required parameters. The purpose of this experiment was to optimize the synthesis of these nanoparticles for glioblastoma treatment applications. The nanoparticles were synthesized using emulsion polymerization via ARGET ATRP synthesis, a technique that allows for control over chain length and small amounts of catalyst. The organic monomers were emulsified with crosslinker, surfactants, and ATRP reagents and reduced in an oxygen-free environment. They were then purified through centrifuging and their size/charge properties were characterized through DLS and zeta potential techniques, respectively. Varying experimental factors affected the properties of the nanoparticles. It was found that increased initiator and reducing agent concentrations resulted in a loss of swelling capabilities but increased surfactant concentration led to smaller nanoparticles. The results indicate successful synthesis of the desired nanoparticles, but further experimentation is required to confirm the properties, chemical composition, and reproducibility of these particles as well as their potential as therapeutic agents.

title: KRAS Digital PCR Screening Optimization for the Detection of KRAS Mutations in CTCs and Exosomes in Patients with Pancreatic Cancer
abstract: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) and exosomes can be identified in the peripheral blood of patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), and can inform cancer diagnosis and treatment effect, thus avoiding an invasive primary tumor biopsy. CTCs are rare cells shed from a tumor and into the blood stream, increasing the risk of metastasis. Exosomes are secreted extracellular vesicles that carry proteins and RNA. For this investigation, samples from patients with PDAC were processed using the Labyrinth, a high-throughput microfluidic CTC isolation device, and exosomes were obtained through ultracentrifugation. After isolation, we used digital PCR (dPCR) to screen the CTCs and exosomes for the presence of KRAS mutations, which occur in >90% of PDAC primary tumors. dPCR is an ultrasensitive technique enabling single molecule detection, critical in low input samples. Here, we present the optimization and validation of a KRAS mutation detection assay for CTCs and exosomes, which simultaneously screens for the 7 most frequent clinically detected mutations in the G12/G13 region of the KRAS gene. We compared master mixes (Bio-Rad Supermix vs TaqMan Genotyping), varied concentrations of KRAS screening assay primers and probes, tested lower concentrations of cell spike samples to mimic patient samples, and did a comparative analysis of the assay’s effectiveness in CTCs and exosomes. We also report our initial findings in patient samples. Preferred results include a combination and balance of high levels of amplification as well as detectable separation between wild type (WT), mutation, and empty PCR reaction droplets. Ultimately, this assay could be used to screen high risk patients for development of PDAC and improve cancer care.

title: Fiber Density Promotes Tip Cell Formation to Initiate Angiogenesis
abstract: Angiogenesis is the process of extending microvasculature from pre-existing blood vessels and plays a critical role in development, tissue homeostasis, and disease progression. This process is initiated when normally quiescent endothelial cells lining the walls of blood vessels transition into activated tip cells that can degrade and invade the surrounding extracellular matrix (ECM). Invading tip cells then lead trailing stalk cells to collectively migrate, eventually resulting in the formation of patent neovessels. While many pro-angiogenic soluble factors have been identified, how physical properties of the ECM influence tip cell formation remains less explored. Here, we engineered a microfluidic 3D tip cell formation assay composed of a lumenized endothelialized arteriole-scale channel fully embedded in a user-defined ECM. To examine the influence of matrix fibers on mediating tip cell formation, we integrated fiber-reinforced fibrin hydrogels with this assay. Briefly, linear high-molecular-weight dextran (86 kDa) was functionalized with vinyl sulfone (a UV-initiated photocrosslinkable group) and dissolved at 0.6 g ml -1 in Milli-Q water and dimethylformamide with 0.015% Irgacure 2959 photoinitiator. This polymer solution was electrospun into fiber mats and selectively photocrosslinked and processed into fiber segments with tunable diameter, length, and stiffness that were functionalized for cell adhesion with the peptide CGRGDS. Embedding fiber segments within fibrin hydrogels enabled tunability of fiber density independent of fibrin weight % (allowing us to maintain a constant bulk hydrogel density, stiffness, and pore size). We found that increasing the density of fibers enhanced tip cell formation and invasion into fibrin hydrogels. Supportive of an endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, tip cells in our assay exhibited traits associated with mesenchymal cells including migratory capacity, the ability to degrade the surrounding matrix, development of actomyosin-protrusions, and loss of vascular endothelial cadherin. Taken together, this work investigates how fiber density, an important physical attribute of the ECM, regulates tip cell formation and suggests that a fibrous topography promotes the transition of quiescent endothelial cells towards a mesenchymal phenotype. A greater understanding of the mechanobiology underlying tip cell formation and function is critical to our understanding of angiogenesis and in the future could aid in the development of pro-angiogenic therapies and implantable biomaterials.

title: Synthesis and Characterization of Poly(hydroxyethyl methacrylate) (PHEMA) Hydrogels for Drug Delivery Applications
abstract: Nanoparticle based drugs offer immense possibilities as a next-generation medical technology, but currently lack a nontoxic, reliable method of targeted delivery. Due to its biocompatible nature, flexible cross-linked structure, and numerous accessible hydrogen bonding sites, PHEMA hydrogels may be viable candidates as encapsulating materials for targeted nanodrug delivery. The primary objectives of this study are the systemic synthesis of PHEMA hydrogels via radical polymerization of and the multimodal materials characterization of PHEMA hydrogels. Material and structural properties of the PHEMA hydrogels were evaluated using scanning electron microscopy, fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, and ultraviolet visible spectroscopy. The influence of pH on hydrogel swelling behavior over a period of 48 hours was investigated in this study. To verify its efficacy as a targeted drug-delivery agent, PHEMA hydrogel’s overall retention and release of iron oxide nanoparticles was measured through dynamic light scattering and ultraviolet visible spectroscopy. The results of this study will be highly significant in the design of higher-efficacy vehicles for targeted drug delivery.

title: Elucidating Metabolism of E. coli double Knockout Strains
abstract: Determining the metabolic effects of gene knockouts in workhorse microorganisms such as Escherichia coli is an important topic for metabolic engineering since it allows for the elucidation of kinetic limitations within those organisms that are essential to understand when designing them in industrial contexts. Most studies in the past have focused on strains with single gene knockouts; this project extends this analysis to double knockouts, which are significant since they allow for the restriction of fluxes to one of the three glycolytic pathways present in E. coli and the complete elimination of reactions catalyzed by multiple isozymes. In this study, adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) was performed on Δ pgi Δ gnd , Δ pgi Δ edd , and Δ rpiA Δ rpiB double knockouts for around 1 month to maximize their growth rates on minimal medium with glucose. At the end of this time, they were grown with 13 C-containing glucose tracers, their amino acids and carbohydrates were collected and analyzed with GC-MS, and the isotopic labelling implied by the GC-MS data was used to reconstruct metabolic fluxes using the Metran metabolic flux analysis software. A comparison was made between the glucose uptake-normalized and absolute fluxes of the Δ pgi Δ edd strain. Future work will include continuing this ALE for a longer time period and with more sets of gene knockouts, as well as sequencing the genomes of the evolved cells to determine which mutations allow them to grow faster.

title: Systematic Exploration of Peg-Grafted Polyelectrolytes for Intracellular Drug Delivery
abstract: The cellular and endosomal membranes represent a significant delivery barrier in cytosolically active therapeutics. To address this challenge, several investigators have developed cationic and pH-responsive self-assembling polymeric nanoparticles as a drug delivery vehicle to enhance cellular uptake and endosomal escape of drug cargoes into the cytosol. To date, these approaches have largely leveraged homopolymers or block copolymer architectures – as such, design rules for other polymer architectures remain poorly characterized. For this project, we fill that gap with exploration of a PEG-grafted copolymer system. Libraries of poly[poly(ethylene glycol) methyl ether methacrylate-co-butyl methacrylate-co-(2-diethylamino) ethyl methacrylate] (PEGMA-co-EB) graft copolymers with varying hydrophobic molecular weight, hydrophilic volume fraction and graft lengths was synthesized and characterized. They were then screened for hydrodynamic sizes, endosomolytic activity and drug delivery competency in vitro . Promising formulations were applied in a murine B16.F10 melanoma utilizing 2’4’-cGAMP, a STING agonist, as the therapeutic agent and cargo. From our in vitro experiments, we discovered that formulations with low hydrophilic volume fraction (W PEG ~ 20%), moderate hydrophobic molecular weight (MW ~ 30 kDa), and short graft lengths (MW PEG ~ 300 Da) self-assembles into larger-sized particles and exhibit superior bioactivity. These formulations, when applied to our in vivo tumor model, were able to better slow tumor growth compared to our free drug control. Collectively, our results highlighted design rules for application of a cationic graft copolymer structure for drug delivery, and adding understanding of another tool in the drug delivery arsenal.

title: Scaling Down DNA-Based Information Storage
abstract: DNA offers extremely dense and long-term information storage capabilities, enabling the ability to accommodate growing data storage needs as a potentially transformative archival medium. Recent advancements in DNA synthesis and sequencing have created the potential for storage systems of useful sizes 1,2 . Here, we focus on miniaturizing the storage of DNA files through the development of a microfluidic device capable of selective file separations 3,4 . Our design creates polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) microfluidic reaction chambers to extract specific files using chemical handles and modified magnetic beads. We optimize the system for bead mobility across an incorporated air gap that allows for an effective physical separation of the desired file. To visually demonstrate strand retrieval, we capture 20 nucleotide (nt) fluorescently labeled primers and track them using fluorescence microscopy. We then expand to double stranded DNAs with variable lengths and show successful and specific file recovery by fragment analyzer and qPCR analyses. After file separation, we determined that the remaining solution is unaltered and can be recycled to the storage library for future use. This system provides potential physical designs for automatable and reusable DNA storage devices. References Takahashi, N. C., et al. Demonstration of End-to-End Automation of DNA Data Storage. title: Exploring a Missing Mechanism That Links Redox Signaling to the Actin Cytoskeleton
abstract: In the cell, reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the actin cytoskeleton work together to control a large range of activities, such as immune response, neural growth, formation of blood vessels, and spreading of cancer cells. However, our understanding of how ROS crosstalks to actin is very limited which has hindered the development of intervening agents. My project is to determine the biochemical mechanism by which a major generator of ROS molecules named NOX and a central regulator of the actin cytoskeleton named WAVE interact with each other. This interaction may serve as a key linkage between ROS and actin in the cell. To understand this mechanism, we use recombinant protein production and various biochemical assays to determine if and how a protein named p47phox can serve as a bridge to bring NOX and WAVE together. We design various mutant proteins to map the regions responsible for p47phox binding to NOX and WAVE, respectively. We also test if p47phox binding to the WAVE Regulatory Complex (WRC) to promote formation of the actin cytoskeleton. This knowledge will help in the understanding of how the cell coordinates ROS signaling and the actin cytoskeleton to drive various processes and has the potential to reveal new targets for therapeutic development.

title: CRISPR Screen to Investigate Contributors to Paracellular Barrier Formation in Vitro
abstract: Barrier-forming cells fulfil an important role in the body by regulating paracellular transport and ultimately protecting homeostasis. To elucidate potential participants in paracellular barrier formation, we performed an arrayed CRISPR knockout screen across 8400 human genes. For the screen, we used Caco2 cells, an immortalized barrier-forming gut epithelial cell line. Our Caco2 cells constitutively express Cas-9 and are robust enough to tolerate high-throughput screening conditions. The Caco2 cells were seeded at a defined density in transfection medium into 96-well plates containing the arrayed gRNA. The cells underwent reverse transfection for 24-hours before Anti-Anti was added to the media to protect against contamination. The cells were maintained in culture for four days before we induced the barrier by switching to Neurobasal media. After six days in Neurobasal media, the cells were fixed and stained for ZO-1, a tight-junction protein that localizes to the paracellular membrane in barrier-forming cells. Each well was then imaged in a Z-stack in four locations with the ImageXpress Micro XL. The screen was performed in two replicates across 109 plates. Images from both replicates were analyzed with MATLAB code to quantify variation in barrier continuity and tortuosity. Positive hits from the screen will be confirmed and tested for barrier permeability in our human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB) model and a Zebrafish model.

title: Role of Tissue Geometry in Regulating Liver Bud Morphogenesis
abstract: Fetal liver development is a multicellular morphogenetic process that transforms an initial hepatic bud into liver tissue. A pivotal point during development occurs when the hepatic bud forms and migrates into the surrounding mesenchyme to begin rapid spatiotemporal liver growth. This particular transient stage of liver development is due to many local biomechanical signaling mechanisms that regulate hepatic architecture and migration. However, complete knowledge of this phenomenon is still insufficient. Through the application of bioengineering principles, current research looks to examine how micro-environmental matrix stiffness stimulates hepatic bud formation and migration into the mesenchyme. Our approach utilizes an in vitro model of the fetal liver bud via 3D spheroidal and toroidal culture of a model hepatic cell line (HepG2) to determine how liver bud geometry influences subsequent cell proliferation. HepG2 cells are seeded into round bottom ULA (ultra-low attachment) plates and microtissue 3D ™ devices to form compact spheroids and toroid tissues (72 hours) respectively. These tissues after harvesting are embedded into varying concentrations of Matrigel (growth factor positive) as a model of the local hepatic mesenchyme to determine an association between matrix stiffness and cellular migration. Preliminary data suggests a strong correlation between tissue geometry and migration of cells in varying concentrations of matrix. This project proposes new insights into the biomechanical mechanisms that promote liver development.

title: Bioreactor Design for the Maturation and Organization of Engineered Cardiac Patches
abstract: Introduction: About 40,000 babies are born with a congenital heart defect (CHD) every year in the United States. Approximately 25% of these babies require surgery within their first year. The current materials available to surgeons for the reconstruction of CHDs are exclusively acellular and inert, limiting the size and location of patched repair and often lead to arrhythmias. Living engineered cardiac patches (ECPs) that integrate with the heart could reduce arrhythmias and allow for more extensive repairs. In vivo native cardiac tissue consists of highly organized layers and structures. We hypothesize that directional and physiological application of strain, sheer stress, and electrical stimulation can direct ECP maturation, organization, and trabeculation. In this study, we designed a bioreactor capable of presenting directional shear strain and electrical stimulation to ECPs grown in vitro . Methods: A bioreactor was designed using Solidworks to fit three ECPs that measure 8 mm in diameter and 2 mm in height and two carbon electrodes. A fluid mechanics computational model was run in COMSOL Multiphysics in order to determine physiologically relevant flow and pressure profiles. The bioreactor was then 3D-printed using Formlabs’ Dental SG Resin , which is an autoclavable, nontoxic, not biodegradable, nonporous, and UV-transparent material. The final design of the 3D-printed reaction chamber is compatible with the adapters, fittings, and tubing necessary for the full model. Results: The fluid mechanics simulation of the final model showed that the bioreactor supports the targeted physiologically relevant shear stress of 10 dyne/cm 2 . Throughout system operation, laminar flow is maintained as fluid flows across the chamber and perfuses through the ECPs. When in contact with the ECPs, carbon electrodes attached to an electrical source will electrically stimulate the cardiomyocytes to contract simultaneously. The bioreactor was printed using an autoclavable, nontoxic, and non-biodegradable dental resin capable of adjustable pressures, flow profiles, and electrical pacing. Discussion and Conclusion: This study presents a bioreactor chamber that can be 3D-printed out of Dental SG Resin and is shown in computational flow models to maintain physiologic pressures, shear flow, and electrical stimulation through an ECP. Future experiments include flow testing through the device and evaluation of cell viability, proliferation, organization, tissue morphology, vascularization, contractile force, and synchronization. The bioreactor will later be incorporated into a control system that provides automated ECP differentiation and maturation using encapsulated pluripotent stem cells.

title: Modulation of Adjuvant Loading and Degradation Profiles of Biocompatible Polymeric Nanoparticles for Immune Stimulation
abstract: Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) hydrogels are commonly used in reparative tissue engineering and regenerative medicine due to their biocompatibility, hydrophilicity, and slow rate of degradation. Similarly, these desirable properties make PEG diacrylate (PEGDA) nanoparticles (NP) an attractive platform for delivery of therapeutic vaccines. Binding immunostimulatory ligands (adjuvants) to delivery platforms with a slow rate of degradation would encourage long-acting immune stimulation and thereby increase efficacy of vaccines. Therefore, our objective is to characterize the effect of modulus of PEGDA NP on rate of degradation and of NP surface density of CpG ODN for enhanced, sustained immunostimulatory effect. Aminated NPs for ligand attachment were synthesized by first mixing a pre-particle solution, which was emulsified in silicone oil and exposed to UV light to initiate polymerization. Pre-particle solution contained 50% or 30% wt/wt total solids in methanol consisting of 88% crosslinker [PEG diacrylate (PEGDA, Mn=700)], 10% cationic functional monomer [2-aminoethyl methacrylate], 1% photoinitiator [diphenyl(2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl)phosphine oxide (TPO)], and 1% dye [Rhodamine B]. Particle degradation was monitored over 4 weeks using thermogravitational analysis (TGA), dynamic light scattering (DLS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and Rhodamine B release in pH 5, 7.4, and 10 buffers via fluorescence. A bifunctional linker, SMCC (succinimidyl 4-(N-maleimidomethyl) cyclohexane-1-carboxylate) was conjugated to NP free amines and the 5’ modified thiol on CpG. CpG loading was confirmed by UV-Vis spectrophotometry at 260 nm to measure amount of unbound nucleic acid concentration in the supernatant. TGA showed linear decrease in particle mass in both 50% and 30% total solids PEGDA NP formulations of all pH buffers over 4 weeks, suggesting bulk erosion of the polymer matrix of the NP. RITC release in solution increased sharply over week 1 of buffer storage, then was maintained from weeks 1-4. While this is indicative of bulk erosion, previous studies note the high hydrophilicity and small size of RITC could result in diffusive leaching into solution rather than matrix degradation. DLS measurements of hydrodynamic diameter and zeta potential were measured to be 273 ± 4 nm and 23.9 ± 4.9, respectively. The net positive charge of unfunctionalized PEGDA-NP suggest presence of free amines on the NP surface and PEGDA NP were functionalized with CpG ODN of varied surface densities. Overall, this work demonstrated that PEGDA NP exhibit slow degradation profiles similar to those expected for PEG hydrogels. PEGDA NP therefore remain an attractive candidate for long-acting immune stimulation.

title: Engineering Escherichia coli for Methanol-Dependent Growth and Production
abstract: An abundance of methane from natural gas reserves has raised interest in engineering synthetic methylotrophs that can utilize methane or methanol, the oxidized form of methane, for growth and chemical production. Synthetic methylotrophs are non-methylotrophic platform organisms that have been engineered to utilize reduced C1 compounds. Since native methylotrophs lack many of the well-developed genetic engineering tools that platform organisms possess, the development of robust synthetic methylotrophs is of considerable interest. Our lab previously developed a synthetic Escherichia coli methylotroph that consumes 1 mol of methanol with 1 mol of glucose concurrently, making this strain “methanol-dependent.” This allows the sugar feedstock cost to be reduced by supplying a portion of the carbon substrate as methanol, which is less expensive. Using adaptive laboratory evolution and process optimization, we report improvements to growth and acetone production. One such evolved strain exhibited robust methanol-dependent growth in glucose minimal medium, whereas negligible growth was observed using the ancestral strain. To improve acetone production (from acetyl-CoA via enzymes from Clostridium ), yeast extract was supplemented to this minimal medium to provide amino acids for biomass synthesis, allowing methanol and glucose to be used primarily for acetone production. As expected, our data demonstrate that acetone production increases with increasing yeast extract concentration (from 2 to 6 g/L). Future work will involve scale-up to a recently developed cell-recycle bioreactor system for high-titer acetone production at bench-scale. This work expands the knowledge of the synthetic methylotrophy field by highlighting the importance of using reduced C1 compounds, alone or together with sugar-based feedstocks, for the production of liquid fuels and chemicals.

title: Optimizing Production of EV71 Virus-like-Particle from CHO Cells
abstract: EV71 virus-like-particle (VLP) mimics the enterovirus causing hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD), an illness that is prevalent in east and southeast Asia and currently has no specific prevention method or treatment. The EV71 VLP has been shown to elicit the immune response necessary for a promising vaccine. To test the VLP’s feasibility as a vaccine candidate for HFMD, large quantities of it must be isolated. Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells transfected with the EV71 VLP vector used are a unique system in that the cells are capable of continuously producing EV71 VLP without inducing cell lysis, a common problem in cells transfected with other variations of the VLP vector. To optimize EV71 VLP production further, we conditioned expressing CHO cells with dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) or sodium butyrate (NaB) and observed differences in EV71 VLP amounts qualitatively via western blot imaging. Additionally, we performed microtiter BCA assays for total protein quantification to see if this method could be used to quantify the differences in VLP production. The optimal percentage of DMSO for small volume plate cultures (3ml of media) was found to be 2.0%, and the optimal concentration of NaB for 3ml and 10ml plate cultures was found to be 1.0mM. We concluded the BCA assay is an inappropriate method for quantifying VLP production due to its inherent relativity and lack of specificity for the VLP. In the future, obtaining EV71 VLP may be further improved by conditioning simultaneously with DMSO and NaB, by developing a cost-effective method for specifically quantifying EV71 VLP, by scaling up production with CHO cells to larger volumes or suspended culture, and by optimizing purification of the VLP via ion exchange chromatography.

title: Utilizing Endotracheal Tubes to Modulate Particle Deposition Profiles in a 3D-Printed Lung Model
abstract: Design of therapeutics for aerosol delivery relies heavily on the use of deposition profiles of healthy, male patients to predict drug performance and efficiency. Delivery of aerosolized therapeutic using a device such as a nebulizer may be needed while a patient is intubated; however, it is unknown whether the presence of an endotracheal (ET) tube alters the deposition profile of a drug in the lungs. Our objective is to investigate the differences in airflow through the lungs in the presence of an ET tube and determine whether these effects can be tuned through altering parameters such as tube diameter, cuff inflation, and release outlet location to inform the formulation and administration of aerosolized therapeutics. By leveraging our 3D-printing capabilities, we can quantify particle deposition for each of the five lung lobes in an anatomically accurate model derived from patient computed tomography (CT) scans printed using the Carbon M1 3D-Printer. ET tubes with inner diameters (ID) of 7, 8 or 9 mm were compared to a clinical flow profile of a healthy male without an ET tube. Additionally, ET tube depth and cuff shape were altered to skew deposition toward one side of the lung. We found that, while altering depth had little effect on the deposition profile, altering ET tube ID did have a significant impact with the 9 mm ET tube skewing 74% (p = 0.001) of the fluorescent polystyrene 1 μm diameter particles delivered towards the right lung. A similar effect was achieved by altering the inflation of the cuff to direct 70% (p = 0.03) of the delivered particles to the right lung. These effects were also investigated at various flow rates to provide information on the optimal point of release in the breath cycle. Overall, the ID and orientation of an ET tube can have a significant effect on the efficiency of the delivery of aerosolized therapeutics to a specific region of the lung and should be considered when designing pharmaceutics and dosing for intubated patients.

title: Rewiring Amino Acid Biosynthesis Via Regulator Modulation and Operon Overexpression Improves Methanol Utilization in a Synthetic Escherichia coli Methylotroph
abstract: The abundance of natural gas has made reduced one carbon compounds like methane and methanol attractive feedstocks for commodity chemical and fuel production, particularly in bioprocesses where they can replace more expensive sugar substrates. While many organisms natively consume one carbon substrates, these microbes (known as methylotrophs) lack many of the well-developed genetic engineering tools that platform organisms possess, which limits their production capacity. Engineering methylotrophy in industrially popular organisms is a promising alternative – in particular, progress has been made to engineer Escherichia coli to consume methanol. However, to date, no E. coli strain has been developed that can grow on methanol as a sole carbon substrate. We have identified amino acid biosynthesis as a crucial bottleneck to sole methylotrophy using 13 C labelling – while most metabolites in glycolysis and the TCA cycle show substantial methanol incorporation, labelling in amino acids is significantly lower, and many amino acids lack methanol carbon entirely. Starting with an E. coli ΔfrmA variant expressing heterologous ribulose monophosphate (RuMP) pathway enzymes, we achieved greater methanol incorporation into amino acids using a variety of metabolic engineering strategies. Improvements were made by modulating regulators of amino acid biosynthesis, overexpressing enzymes for the biosynthesis of specific amino acids, and utilizing enzyme variants that do not possess traditional allosteric inhibition. The best variants from each method were then combined, yielding additive benefits to methanol incorporation. The resulting strains represent unique starting points for achieving sole methylotrophy via adaptive evolution or further metabolic engineering.

title: Critical Flux during Tangential Flow Microfiltration of Precipitated Proteins
abstract: There is considerable clinical interest in both polyclonal Immunoglobulin G (IgG) and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) as biotherapuetics. Polyclonal IgG is currently purified from blood serum using an ethanol-based precipitation, while the initial step in the purification of most mAbs is by bind-and-elute Protein A affinity chromatography. We have been exploring the use of ZnCl 2 – PEG combinations for continuous precipitation of IgG / mAbs, exploiting the high product titer of current mAb products (>5 g/L). Long term operation of the system can be achieved by operating the membrane unit at a filtrate flux below the critical flux for the onset of fouling. The objective of this particular project was to explore opportunities for increasing the critical flux, including the use of co-flow to provide a more constant transmembrane pressure drop throughout the module. The precipitation of IgG was conducted in a tubular precipitation reactor with sequential inline addition of ZnCl 2 (a crosslinking agent) and PEG (a volume exclusion agent). High IgG yield (>99%) was obtained in the precipitate. The precipitated IgG was then concentrated and washed using hollow fiber polyethersulfone membranes. The critical flux was evaluated using a flux-stepping procedure, with the transmembrane pressure evaluated as a function of time during each constant flux interval. The addition of co-flow did not cause any measurable increase in the critical flux. However, the critical flux could be increased by using membranes with higher permeability. The critical flux was also a function of the aging of the precipitates, with fresh precipitates found to have a larger mean particle size. These results provide important insights into the development of effective tangential flow microfiltration systems for use in continuous protein purification by precipitation.

title: An Electrochemical Biosensor for in-Situ Detection of Lipids By Immobilization of Cholesterol Oxidase
abstract: Atherosclerosis is the blockage of blood flow through arteries due to plaque buildup from high cholesterol. High cholesterol does not display symptoms and can only be detected through a blood test. There is a clinical need for a device able to analyze cholesterol concentration in-situ. For the development of a biosensor for cholesterol detection, an amperometric, three-electrode system was utilized. Cholesterol oxidase (ChOx) was immobilized at the working electrode through a self-assembled monolayer (SAM) of octadecanethiol (ODT) or thioglycolic acid (TGA) and electropolymerization of pyrrole. Multiple immobilization methods were assessed through amperometric measurements and cyclic voltammetry. The cyclic voltammetry experiments were run for assessing the formation of the self-assembled monolayer, by determining a change in current measured by the sensor. The amperometric measurements were conducted for cholesterol detection along with the characterization of sensitivity of the functionalized biosensor. This study looked at different enzyme immobilization methods for creating a device that can analyze cholesterol blood composition. The obtained results show that two functionalization methods yielded different results, with a fairly good liner response curve between the sensor’s current signal and cholesterol concentration for the sensor with the pyrrole method. Future work includes further optimization of the functionalization process and tuning of the sensitivity, among others.

title: Development of Mycobacterium Smegmatis As a Host Strain for Polyketide Synthase Production
abstract: Polyketide synthases (PKSs) are enzymes that synthesize a biologically important family of complex chemicals called polyketides, which include antibiotics, anticancer, and immunosuppressant drugs. Due to their highly complex architectures, polyketides are difficult to synthesize via traditional organic chemistry means. Through bioengineering, scientists are able to genetically modify PKSs to selectively produce polyketides of interest such as adipic acid, methyl ketones, and chiral building blocks. However, commonly used heterologous hosts for PKS production, such as Escherichia coli and Streptomyces, often produce misfolded, truncated, and non-functional PKSs or they can be challenging to genetically manipulate and grow slowly. In response to this need, we seek to develop Mycobacterium smegmatis as a new PKS host due to its more easily manipulated genome, availability of genetic tools, relatively fast growth rate, and ability to naturally produce precursors for biosynthesis. To assay for phosphopantetheinylation, an essential post-translational modification of PKSs made by phosphopantetheinyl transferase (PPTase), we introduced the gene bpsA , which encodes a blue-pigment indigoidine synthetase, into wild type M. smegmatis . We found that wild type M. smegmatis produced indigoidine, which indicates the presence of an active PPTase. Furthermore, we genomically integrated a second copy of a PPTase under the control of a constitutive promoter to improve the ability of the host to phosphopanteheinylate heterologous PKSs and integrated T7 RNA polymerase to make the host compatible with IPTG inducible T7 promoter expression systems. Additionally, we developed an IPTG inducible T7 promoter expression plasmid, containing a his-tagged RFP under an inducible T7 promoter for protein purification. Flow cytometry was used to study the inducibility of the system by measuring fluorescence levels of induced and non-induced M. smegmatis containing the T7 expression plasmid, further providing evidence that these genetic tools will be a useful platform for purifying PKSs or for fermentative production of polyketides.

title: Modeling the Dissolution of Prednisolone Loaded Polyvinyl Alcohol Films
abstract: Prednisolone loaded polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) films were prepared and characterized to find density and glass transition temperature. Drug release and mass loss studies of these films were conducted in order to establish a predictive and tunable model that could be used in order to formulate pills specific to meet unique release requirements. The studies were conducted at different solution volumes (10 mL and 50 mL) at pH 6.8, as well as with and without the surfactant Tween 80 (thought to imitate conditions in the intestines) in order to create a comprehensive drug release system. The addition of Tween 80 allowed for the complete dissolution of the drug in supernatant within 2 hours, while other changes in the surroundings, such as change in volume, and changes to the film, such as film thickness and drug loading, did not largely influence the release kinetics. The experimental results (concentration profile with time) were fitted using the Noyes-Whitney Approximation, a surface erosion drug dissolution model based on Fick’s first law, which produces a good correlation (R 2 > 0.9) with simultaneous prediction of physical parameters, solubility and lumped rate constant. The developed model and experimental procedures for the release of prednisolone from the PVA films will be significant for future film based drug delivery development and design.
